meta.blurb: Omar is fifty-two, and his sister Salma, a physiotherapist, hates hype. Once a month for a year they climb the stone steps of Bell Hill, and she explains what really helps people stay strong and independent as they age.
meta.bible:
Omar: a teacher who turns fifty-two at the start of the story; friendly, a little out of shape, and a grandfather. Salma: his younger sister, a Physiotherapist who loves numbers and hates hype; calm, funny and exact. Bell Hill: the hill with a long flight of stone steps where they walk once a month for a year, from one birthday to the next. Lifespan: the number of years a person lives. Healthspan: the number of those years lived in good health. Stamina, Strength, Balance, Flexibility: the four parts of fitness in this book. World Health Organization: advises adults to do at least 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity a week, or half that of vigorous activity, and muscle-strengthening on at least two days a week. Dementia, Apnoea, Cholesterol, LDL, Osteoporosis, Screening, Physiotherapist, Dietitian: terms used with care. A large international review in 2024 estimated that up to forty-five percent of dementia cases might be prevented or delayed by tackling fourteen risk factors. Facts are hedged: studies often show links and not proof; no medicine or supplement has so far been proven to slow ageing in people; a simple plan beats an expensive one. Safety: people new to hard exercise, with a health condition, an injury or on medicine should ask a doctor first; chest pain, dizziness or sharp pain are signs to stop and get medical advice. This book is general information and is not medical advice. Voice and tone: warm, clear and practical, with a little humour; no invented numbers, studies or quotes; no diagnosis and no personal treatment advice. Added for the full-length book. Nadia: Omar's wife of thirty years, a librarian who loves to cook. Dina: their daughter. Lina: Dina's daughter, aged five, bright and bossy. Hamid: Omar's friend since school, who has a heart attack at fifty-three and recovers. Samira: Hamid's wife. Layla: Omar and Salma's late mother, who broke her hip at seventy-nine. Karim: their late father, who had a serious heart attack at sixty-one. Dr Rahman: Omar's family doctor. Leo: a qualified trainer at the Community Centre. Rosa: runs Rosa's Cafe at the foot of Bell Hill. Mr Okafor: aged seventy-one, leads the Tuesday Walkers. Mr Dalton: a teacher who smokes and later quits. Mrs Hale: aged eighty-three, walks Bell Hill with a stick and tends a street garden. Iris: a woman who uses a wheelchair and lifts weights at the Community Centre. Teo: Omar's guitar teacher. Mr Ford: one of Salma's patients, who slipped and fell. Yusuf: an old friend of Omar. Hill Road School: where Omar teaches. Bell Hill has one hundred and sixty stone steps. The story runs from Omar's birthday in March to the next March, with a walk most months.
 Gil: a quiet widower in the Tuesday Walkers. Hill Road Walkers: the Thursday walking club Omar starts at school. Mrs Hale's street garden is near the foot of Bell Hill. Omar turns fifty-three in the last March of the story.
chapters: One Leg and a Twisted Ankle

beats.scene: Omar blows out candles on a birthday cake while his family claps
beats.summary: Omar turns fifty-two at a family party with his wife Nadia, his daughter Dina and his granddaughter Lina.

beats.scene: Omar stands in a hallway holding a phone with a worried face
beats.summary: During the party a call tells Omar that his old school friend Hamid has had a heart attack.

beats.scene: Omar sits beside a hospital bed where Hamid lies connected to a monitor
beats.summary: Omar visits Hamid, who is awake and frightened and says he never thought it could happen to him.

beats.scene: Omar climbs the stairs of his building and rests on the landing
beats.summary: Climbing his own stairs, Omar realises that he is badly out of breath and has not exercised for years.

beats.scene: Omar and Nadia talk at the kitchen table late at night over tea
beats.summary: Nadia says worrying is not a plan and suggests he ask his sister Salma, who understands bodies.

beats.scene: Salma arrives at the door with a rucksack and a flask
beats.summary: Salma comes the next day, listens, and says she has no magic to offer, only honest evidence.

beats.scene: Salma spreads a map on the table and taps a hill outside town
beats.summary: Salma proposes a bargain: one walk a month for a year up Bell Hill, with one question answered each time.

beats.scene: Omar stands at the bottom of a very long flight of stone steps
beats.summary: On the first walk Omar sees the one hundred and sixty stone steps of Bell Hill and gulps.

beats.scene: Omar halfway up the steps, hands on knees, while Salma checks her watch
beats.summary: Omar climbs and stops four times to catch his breath, and Salma says this is simply his starting point.

beats.scene: Omar and Salma drink tea on a bench at the top above the town
beats.summary: At the top they drink tea and look at the town, and Salma sets the first question: what is a long life for?

beats.scene: Salma draws two lines of different lengths on the back of a map
beats.summary: Salma explains lifespan, the years you live, and healthspan, the years you live in good health.

beats.scene: An older woman sits in an armchair by a window, holding a stick
beats.summary: Their mother Layla broke her hip at seventy-nine and lived years more, but never regained her independence.

beats.scene: Salma points at the gap between the two lines with her finger
beats.summary: In many countries people spend several of their last years in poor health; the aim is to shrink that gap.

beats.scene: Omar sits on a bench with closed eyes, picturing himself as an old man
beats.summary: Salma asks Omar to picture himself at eighty and to plan backwards from what he wants to be doing.

beats.scene: Omar writes a short list on a notepad beside a flask of tea
beats.summary: Omar writes his wishes: to sit on the floor with Lina's children, to walk to the market, and to visit his father's village by the sea.

beats.scene: Salma draws arrows from each wish to a body skill on the notepad
beats.summary: Salma turns each wish into a physical skill: rising from the floor, walking far, carrying a suitcase, climbing stairs.

beats.scene: Two elderly neighbours: one waters plants, one sits indoors by a window
beats.summary: People of the same age can be very different in what they can do; habits explain part of it, never all.

beats.scene: Salma sketches a gently falling line on a notepad
beats.summary: Abilities fade slowly with age, but a person who builds fitness now starts higher and falls more gently.

beats.scene: Omar shows a notepad list to Nadia while Lina bounces on the sofa
beats.summary: Omar shows Nadia his list, and Lina asks whether he will still carry her when she is ten.

beats.scene: Omar sits on the living-room floor, about to try standing without hands
beats.summary: Omar tries to rise from the floor without using his hands and finds that he needs both of them.

beats.scene: Salma draws four arrows on a notepad, each pointing to a disease name
beats.summary: On the April walk Salma names the four big threats: heart and blood-vessel disease, cancer, type 2 diabetes and brain diseases such as dementia.

beats.scene: Salma draws a pipe with yellow deposits narrowing the inside
beats.summary: In heart disease, fatty deposits narrow the arteries, and a blockage can cause a heart attack, as it did for Hamid.

beats.scene: Salma draws many small circles with one dark circle among them
beats.summary: Cancer is many diseases in which cells grow out of control; smoking, alcohol, weight, inactivity and sun change the risk, and screening can find some early.

beats.scene: A glass of sugary drink beside a drawing of a body and a gauge
beats.summary: In type 2 diabetes the body copes badly with blood sugar; extra weight, little movement and poor food raise the risk, and damage builds silently.

beats.scene: Salma draws a simple head shape with a tangle of lines inside
beats.summary: Dementia is a group of brain diseases that harm memory and thinking; it grows commoner with age, and some risks can be lowered.

beats.scene: A young tree stands beside an old tree with thick roots
beats.summary: These diseases build up slowly over decades, long before symptoms, so the habits of midlife matter.

beats.scene: Salma fans out a hand of playing cards on a bench
beats.summary: Genes and luck deal the cards, but habits decide how well you play them and can change the odds a great deal.

beats.scene: Omar looks troubled while Salma places a hand on his arm
beats.summary: Omar says their father Karim had a serious heart attack at sixty-one; Salma says family history raises risk but is a warning, not a sentence.

beats.scene: Salma sits on a log beside a winding path, one hand raised
beats.summary: Nobody can promise anything: some who ignore their health live long and some who do everything right fall ill young, but a good plan improves the odds.

beats.scene: Hamid, thinner and smiling, sits at a kitchen table with a leaflet
beats.summary: Hamid comes home from hospital and starts a rehabilitation programme, telling Omar that the heart attack was years in the making.

beats.scene: Salma chalks four words on a flat stone beside the path
beats.summary: A fit body has four parts: stamina, strength, balance and flexibility.

beats.scene: Omar jogs on the spot with a puzzled face while Salma shakes her head
beats.summary: Omar thought fitness meant running; Salma says it is a mix, since a runner can be weak and a lifter breathless.

beats.scene: Omar pauses halfway up the steps, breathing hard, one hand on the rail
beats.summary: Stamina is the fitness of heart and lungs, how long you can keep going before you must stop.

beats.scene: Salma shows a notepad graph with rising lines to Omar
beats.summary: In large studies, people with higher stamina tend to live longer; studies show a link, not proof.

beats.scene: Two walkers stride briskly side by side along a country road
beats.summary: The World Health Organization advises adults to do at least 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity a week, or half that of vigorous activity.

beats.scene: Omar breathes hard but keeps talking as he walks beside Salma
beats.summary: The talk test: during moderate effort you breathe harder but can talk; during hard effort only a few words.

beats.scene: Omar strolls along a street whistling while Salma shakes her head
beats.summary: Omar's usual stroll fails the talk test, since he could sing, but a brisk walk with Salma passes it.

beats.scene: Omar marks walks on a wall calendar in his kitchen
beats.summary: Omar plans to walk briskly for thirty minutes on five days a week, to school and on Sundays with Nadia.

beats.scene: Omar walks to school in the morning light, past parked cars
beats.summary: In the first weeks his calves ache and he arrives damp, but he soon sleeps better and finds the walk easier.

beats.scene: Omar and Nadia walk fast along a river on a sunny Sunday, talking
beats.summary: On a Sunday walk Omar and Nadia chat easily while walking fast, and Omar feels his stamina beginning to grow.

beats.scene: Salma holds up a stopwatch beside a sunny picnic spot on the hill
beats.summary: At the June walk Salma explains that short bursts of hard effort can raise fitness faster for the time spent.

beats.scene: Omar strides hard along the path, red in the face, mouth open
beats.summary: Hard effort means quick, deep breathing and only a few words at a time; it should feel hard but never impossible.

beats.scene: Salma raises one finger in warning while Omar nods seriously
beats.summary: People new to hard exercise, or with a health condition, an injury or regular medicine, should ask a doctor first.

beats.scene: Dr Rahman listens to Omar's chest with a stethoscope in a bright room
beats.summary: Dr Rahman examines Omar, asks about his father, and says more exercise is wise if he builds up gradually.

beats.scene: Dr Rahman writes a short list on a card and hands it over
beats.summary: She lists the signs to stop and get help: chest pain, fainting, dizziness, unusual breathlessness and sharp pain.

beats.scene: Omar speeds along a park path while Lina rides a scooter beside him
beats.summary: Omar tries his first intervals, one fast minute and two easy, four times, while Lina cheers.

beats.scene: Omar stops at the side of the path with his hands on his hips
beats.summary: Omar overdoes the second week, feels exhausted, and learns to start slowly and add a little each week.

beats.scene: Omar rubs a sore thigh at the kitchen table while Nadia pours tea
beats.summary: Aching muscles after exercise are normal; sharp, sudden or worsening pain is a reason to stop.

beats.scene: Salma draws a mountain with a wide base and a small peak
beats.summary: Most training should be easy, with only one or two hard sessions a week, and rest days are when the body grows stronger.

beats.scene: Omar climbs the school stairs two at a time while pupils watch
beats.summary: By the end of June Omar climbs his stairs without stopping, and his pupils notice that he moves faster.

beats.scene: Salma lifts a heavy rucksack from the path with a straight back
beats.summary: At the July walk Salma shows how to lift with a straight back and bent knees and introduces strength.

beats.scene: A drawing of a muscle slowly shrinking over the years on a notepad
beats.summary: After about thirty, most people slowly lose muscle unless they use it, though muscle responds to training at almost any age.

beats.scene: An older man rises easily from an armchair, smiling
beats.summary: Strong muscles keep people independent: rising from a chair, carrying shopping, climbing stairs and getting up from the floor.

beats.scene: A drawing of muscle, bone and joint with arrows showing support
beats.summary: Muscles also protect joints and bones, and working muscle uses sugar from the blood.

beats.scene: Omar lifts a water bottle in each hand beside a kitchen chair
beats.summary: Strength training on at least two days a week is advised; body weight, bags, bands or weights all count and no gym is needed.

beats.scene: Omar squeezes a hand grip tester while Salma writes down the number
beats.summary: Simple tests such as grip strength give clues about strength, but they are only clues.

beats.scene: Omar stands up from a chair with crossed arms while Salma times him
beats.summary: Omar's chair-stand test gives average numbers, and he feels relieved to know them.

beats.scene: Leo shows Omar a chair squat in a bright community centre hall
beats.summary: Omar has a first lesson with Leo, a trainer at the Community Centre, who says technique comes before weight.

beats.scene: Omar does a wall push-up while Lina counts on her fingers
beats.summary: At home Omar does chair squats, wall push-ups and rows with a rucksack of books, while Lina counts.

beats.scene: Hamid lifts a small dumbbell while a nurse watches closely
beats.summary: With his doctor's approval Hamid lifts light weights in rehab, and both men add a little each week.

beats.scene: Salma holds a drawing of two bones, one thick and one thin
beats.summary: Bone is living tissue that grows stronger when it carries weight and is pulled by working muscles.

beats.scene: A plate of fish and beans beside a glass of milk
beats.summary: Calcium, vitamin D and protein help bones; very weak bones, called osteoporosis, are a matter for a doctor.

beats.scene: Salma sits beside Mr Ford, whose wrist is in a cast
beats.summary: Falls are a leading cause of injury in older people; Mr Ford slipped on a wet kitchen floor and broke his wrist.

beats.scene: Omar stands on one leg beside a kitchen counter, arms held wide
beats.summary: Balance can be practised: Omar tries standing on one leg at the kitchen counter and manages only about five seconds.

beats.scene: Slow-moving people practise tai chi on the grass in a park at dawn
beats.summary: Balance programmes, including tai chi, can reduce falls in older people; Omar watches a class in the park.

beats.scene: Omar bends toward his toes beside a park bench
beats.summary: Joints stay easier to use when moved through their full range; Omar can reach only as far as his knees.

beats.scene: Omar sits on the carpet with Lina and gets up with one hand
beats.summary: Gentle stretching and everyday movement keep joints supple; Omar practises getting down to the floor and up again with Lina.

beats.scene: Omar chases a red ball across a park, his foot catching a hole
beats.summary: On a hot afternoon in late July, Omar runs after Lina's ball, steps in a hole and twists his ankle.

beats.scene: A swollen ankle raised on a cushion beside a bag of ice
beats.summary: Salma says to rest, raise and protect the ankle; Dr Rahman finds a bad sprain and not a break.

beats.scene: Omar sits at a cafe table, bandaged foot raised, looking up at the hill
beats.summary: The August walk becomes tea at Rosa's Cafe; Salma says setbacks happen and weak balance and ankles were part of the problem.

beats.scene: Omar sits in an armchair, bandaged foot raised, a clock on the wall
beats.summary: Stuck at home with his ankle, Omar sits for hours, and Salma warns that long periods of sitting are linked with poorer health.

beats.scene: A drawing of a seated person with an arrow of rising risk
beats.summary: Studies link long hours of sitting with higher risks of heart disease, diabetes and early death, especially in people who exercise very little.

beats.scene: A kitchen timer on a school desk beside a stack of exercise books
beats.summary: The advice is to break up sitting every half hour with a minute or two of standing or walking; Omar sets a timer.

beats.scene: Omar lifts a bag of rice above his head while seated in a chair
beats.summary: While the ankle heals, Omar trains what is not injured with seated arm and trunk exercises, with medical advice coming first.

beats.scene: Omar takes his first careful steps on flat ground with a bandaged ankle
beats.summary: As the ankle heals, Omar restarts gently: five minutes of flat walking, then ten, without heroics.

beats.scene: Lina hands Omar a small step counter tied with a big ribbon
beats.summary: Dina and Lina give Omar a step counter; even with short walks he averages only about four thousand steps a day.

beats.scene: Salma draws a rising line that flattens out, marked with step numbers
beats.summary: In studies, health benefits rise with daily steps and seem to level off at roughly seven to ten thousand.

beats.scene: An old advertisement for a step counter with a big number on it
beats.summary: Ten thousand is not a magic number: it is widely said to come from an old Japanese advertising slogan, not from a study.

beats.scene: Omar and Nadia walk along a quiet street at dusk after dinner
beats.summary: Omar adds steps by pacing on the phone, taking stairs, parking farther away and walking with Nadia after dinner.

beats.scene: Omar climbs the stone steps of Bell Hill slowly with Salma beside him
beats.summary: At the end of August Omar climbs Bell Hill again, slower than in June and with two stops; losing some ground after an injury is normal.

beats.scene: A person sleeps peacefully in a dark bedroom with the moon at the window
beats.summary: At the September walk Salma says we spend about a third of life asleep, and most adults need seven to nine hours.

beats.scene: A tired man yawns over a cup of coffee at a school desk
beats.summary: Poor sleep is linked with heart disease, diabetes, low mood, accidents and poor memory, and people who sleep too little often do not notice.

beats.scene: A bedside clock showing the same early time each morning
beats.summary: Good sleep begins with regular times: bed and waking at about the same hour every day, weekends included.

beats.scene: A cool dark bedroom with thick curtains drawn across the window
beats.summary: A dark, quiet, cool bedroom helps sleep; Omar buys thick curtains, covers a red light and opens the window.

beats.scene: Omar drinks his morning tea on a sunny balcony
beats.summary: Morning light helps set the body's clock; late caffeine, big late meals and alcohol can all disturb sleep.

beats.scene: A phone charging on a hallway table while a bedroom stays dark
beats.summary: Bright screens late at night can make it harder to fall asleep; Omar charges his phone in the hallway.

beats.scene: Nadia nudges Omar awake as he snores in bed
beats.summary: Nadia says Omar snores loudly and seems to stop breathing at times; Salma says it may be sleep apnoea, which a doctor can check.

beats.scene: Dr Rahman hands Omar a small box with a finger sensor
beats.summary: Dr Rahman arranges a home sleep test; the result shows nothing worrying, though for others such tests lead to useful treatment.

beats.scene: A sleep diary open on a table beside an alarm clock and a pencil
beats.summary: A sleep diary shows Omar his patterns; after a few weeks he falls asleep faster and wakes before the alarm.

beats.scene: Omar naps in an armchair under a blanket in afternoon light
beats.summary: A short early nap can refresh, but a long late nap may spoil night sleep; sleep is a main part of the plan, not a reward.

beats.scene: A table with a plate of vegetables, fish, beans and bread
beats.summary: At the October walk Salma says to eat mostly whole foods and less of the highly processed kind.

beats.scene: A shelf of bright packets beside a basket of fresh vegetables
beats.summary: Large studies link diets high in highly processed food with poorer health, though cause is hard to prove.

beats.scene: A family shares a meal of olive oil, bread, tomatoes and fish
beats.summary: The pattern kept up for years matters more than any single food; Mediterranean-style eating is linked with less heart disease.

beats.scene: Omar and Nadia read a food label in a shop aisle, baskets in hand
beats.summary: Omar and Nadia shop differently: reading labels and choosing beans, lentils, oats and frozen vegetables, which are cheap.

beats.scene: Eggs, fish, beans and yoghurt on a kitchen counter
beats.summary: Some experts suggest older adults need a little more protein to keep muscle; people with kidney disease should ask a doctor first.

beats.scene: A bowl of oats and beans beside fresh fruit and dark bread
beats.summary: Fibre from vegetables, fruit, beans and whole grains is good for the heart and gut; Omar adds a vegetable to every meal.

beats.scene: A glass of water beside a can of sugary drink in a school canteen
beats.summary: Sugary drinks add a lot of sugar with little benefit; water, tea and coffee without much sugar are better choices.

beats.scene: A magazine cover promising a miracle diet, crossed out with a red pen
beats.summary: Fad diets promise miracles, but a plan you cannot keep for years is a poor plan; evidence on fasting is mixed.

beats.scene: Salma measures Omar's waist with a soft tape at the middle
beats.summary: Fat deep around the belly is linked with heart disease and type 2 diabetes; a waist smaller than half a person's height is a rough guide.

beats.scene: Omar writes a small goal on the fridge calendar with a pencil
beats.summary: Omar sets a gentle goal, knowing that weight and waist are not the whole story and that muscle counts too.

beats.scene: Salma and Omar climb the hill in cold bright light, their breath visible
beats.summary: At the November walk Salma says the most dangerous conditions are silent, so a few simple measurements are worth knowing.

beats.scene: A nurse holds a small glucose meter beside a fingertip
beats.summary: High blood sugar over many years can damage the body; a simple blood test shows it, and a doctor explains the result.

beats.scene: Omar rolls up his sleeve while a nurse prepares a blood test
beats.summary: Omar has blood tests at the clinic, early and without breakfast, and looks away like most grown men.

beats.scene: A blood pressure cuff on a man's arm in a bright clinic
beats.summary: High blood pressure usually has no symptoms but raises the risk of heart attack, stroke and kidney disease; it is easy to measure and treat.

beats.scene: Dr Rahman fastens a cuff on Omar's arm as he sits quietly
beats.summary: Dr Rahman measures Omar's pressure; it is a little higher than she likes, so she asks him to measure at home for a week.

beats.scene: Salma draws pipes with yellow deposits and little drops labelled LDL
beats.summary: Some cholesterol, especially LDL, can build up in artery walls; a blood test shows the level and a doctor explains it.

beats.scene: Dr Rahman explains a printed results sheet to Omar, pointing with a pen
beats.summary: Omar's blood sugar is normal and his LDL a little higher than ideal; Dr Rahman suggests food and exercise changes and a recheck in three months.

beats.scene: Omar sits with a home blood pressure monitor and a notebook at dawn
beats.summary: Omar's home readings are lower than the clinic's, since being nervous in a clinic can push pressure up.

beats.scene: Salma shakes her head over a long list of tests on a brochure
beats.summary: More testing is not always better: some tests find harmless things and cause worry; ask what a result would change.

beats.scene: A small card in a wallet with a few numbers written in pencil
beats.summary: Omar keeps a card with his key numbers and test dates; knowing your numbers is not the same as fearing them.

beats.scene: A wall calendar with several appointment dates circled in blue
beats.summary: Screening tests look for certain diseases early, and many countries invite people at set ages; the invitations are worth accepting.

beats.scene: Nadia sits in a waiting room with a leaflet, smiling calmly
beats.summary: Nadia goes for a breast screening appointment, offered in a certain age range in many countries, and the result is clear.

beats.scene: Omar looks suspiciously at a small home test kit on the kitchen table
beats.summary: In some countries people Omar's age are invited to do a bowel screening test at home; he jokes, does it, and the result is normal.

beats.scene: Salma counts tests on her fingers while Omar listens carefully
beats.summary: Other tests include cervical screening and skin checks; for some cancers, such as prostate, experts disagree about routine testing, so it is a talk with a doctor.

beats.scene: A balance scale with benefits on one pan and worries on the other
beats.summary: Screening has benefits and costs: no test is perfect and false alarms happen, but for the main programmes experts judge the benefits to be greater.

beats.scene: Mr Dalton smokes outside the school gate and glances at Omar
beats.summary: Mr Dalton, a colleague who smokes, asks what has changed in Omar; Salma says not smoking is among the best things anyone can do and quitting helps at any age.

beats.scene: Omar leaves a leaflet for a stop-smoking service on Mr Dalton's desk
beats.summary: Support such as stop-smoking services and nicotine replacement makes quitting more likely to work; many people need several attempts.

beats.scene: A glass of water beside an untouched glass of wine at a family table
beats.summary: For alcohol, health bodies agree that less is better, and limits differ by country; Omar adds alcohol-free days.

beats.scene: A seat belt, a sun hat and a cycle helmet on a table
beats.summary: Seat belts, helmets, sun protection and working smoke alarms prevent harm with little effort.

beats.scene: Omar rolls up a sleeve for an injection while a nurse smiles
beats.summary: Vaccines recommended by health services prevent serious illness; Omar asks Dr Rahman which are meant for him and books one.

beats.scene: Omar sits quietly on a frosty bench at the top of the hill
beats.summary: At the December walk Omar says his greatest fear is losing his mind and forgetting Lina; Salma says dementia is not a normal part of ageing.

beats.scene: Omar searches his pockets for his keys while Salma smiles
beats.summary: Forgetting keys is common at any age and is not dementia; lasting changes that affect daily life are a reason to see a doctor.

beats.scene: Salma writes the number fourteen on a notepad and circles it
beats.summary: A 2024 international review estimated that up to 45 percent of dementia cases might be prevented or delayed by tackling fourteen risk factors.

beats.scene: Salma lists items on a notepad: hearing, blood pressure, sugar, cholesterol
beats.summary: The first risk factors: high blood pressure, high LDL cholesterol, diabetes, smoking, alcohol, inactivity, excess weight and hearing loss.

beats.scene: Salma writes the rest of the list: head injury, low mood, pollution
beats.summary: The rest: head injury, depression, loneliness, air pollution, poor eyesight and little schooling early in life.

beats.scene: Salma draws a question mark above a graph with a dotted line
beats.summary: The honest limits: studies show links, not proof, and 45 percent is an estimate, but the steps are good for health anyway.

beats.scene: Omar wears big headphones and presses a button in a quiet hearing booth
beats.summary: Omar has a hearing test; it shows a mild loss of the highest sounds, which explains his trouble in noisy rooms.

beats.scene: An audiologist fits a small hearing aid behind an older man's ear
beats.summary: Untreated hearing loss is linked with a higher risk of dementia; whether hearing aids lower the risk is still being studied, but they help people join in.

beats.scene: An optician points at a letter chart while Omar reads aloud
beats.summary: Poor eyesight is linked with falls and dementia; regular eye tests catch treatable problems, and Omar needs reading glasses.

beats.scene: Omar and Salma look out from the hilltop at the winter sunset
beats.summary: Salma says body and brain are one system; before the next walk Omar is to start learning something new.

beats.scene: Omar holds an old guitar in a small music room at the Community Centre
beats.summary: Omar chooses the guitar, an old wish, and signs up for lessons with a teacher called Teo at the Community Centre.

beats.scene: Omar winces as he presses the strings with sore fingertips
beats.summary: At the first lesson Omar's fingertips hurt and his chords buzz, but Teo says that this is how every beginner starts.

beats.scene: Salma and Omar climb the steps of Bell Hill in cold January air
beats.summary: On the January walk Salma says that learning new, demanding things keeps the brain active and that people who stay mentally busy tend to have lower dementia risk.

beats.scene: Omar looks at a brain-training app on a phone while Salma shakes her head
beats.summary: Brain-training apps make people better at the games, but the evidence that this carries over to everyday memory is weak; real learning is better.

beats.scene: Omar writes a list titled hard, new, regular on a notepad
beats.summary: Good learning is new, hard enough to make you stretch, and practised often in short sessions.

beats.scene: Lina sits on Omar's lap and plucks the guitar strings
beats.summary: At home Lina pushes the strings of the guitar and demands a song, and Omar learns his first tune for her.

beats.scene: Mrs Hale walks slowly up the stone steps with a stick
beats.summary: On the hill Omar meets Mrs Hale, aged eighty-three, who walks up Bell Hill with a stick two mornings a week.

beats.scene: Mrs Hale kneels beside a raised bed of herbs on a city street
beats.summary: Mrs Hale tends a garden bed on her street and says she started growing vegetables at seventy-five.

beats.scene: Omar kneels in soil and digs while Mrs Hale points with her stick
beats.summary: Gardening mixes gentle movement, fresh air and daylight; heavy digging can count as strength work, though it must be done with care.

beats.scene: Omar plays three chords on a bench at the top while walkers listen
beats.summary: Omar plays his first tune on the hilltop; Salma says it is the doing, not the cleverness, that keeps the brain healthy.

beats.scene: Salma and Omar sit on a bench and watch other walkers pass in pairs
beats.summary: Salma says loneliness is linked with a higher risk of early death, heart disease and dementia.

beats.scene: Mrs Hale waters her street garden and smiles at a passing child

B1B2: Omar turns fifty-two on a Saturday in March, and the whole family comes to dinner. His wife Nadia bakes the cake, and his five-year-old granddaughter Lina insists on blowing out every candle for him.
In the middle of the party, Omar's phone rings with bad news. His oldest friend Hamid, who is only fifty-three, has had a heart attack and is in hospital.
Next morning Omar visits Hamid, who is awake but pale and frightened. His friend says quietly that he never thought this could happen to him, because he felt perfectly well the day before.
That evening Omar climbs the stairs to his flat and has to stop for breath on the landing. He realises that he has not exercised for years, and that he has never really thought about his health.

Late that night, Nadia tells Omar that worrying is not enough and that he should do something. She suggests asking his younger sister Salma, a physiotherapist, who understands bodies better than anyone they know.
Salma arrives the next day with a rucksack and a flask of tea, and she listens without interrupting. Then she says that she has no magic and no secret, only honest evidence about what helps.
Salma spreads a map on the table and taps a hill outside town. Her bargain is simple: one walk a month up Bell Hill for a year, with one honest question answered each time.
At the foot of Bell Hill, Omar looks up at the long flight of stone steps. There are one hundred and sixty of them, and they seem to go straight up into the clouds.
Omar climbs bravely, but he has to stop four times to catch his breath. Salma only smiles and says that this is not a failure, because it is simply his starting point.
At the top they share the tea from Salma's flask and look down at the town. Before they walk down, she asks the first question: what is a long life actually for?
On the back of the map, Salma draws two lines of different lengths. The long one is lifespan, the number of years you live, and the shorter one is healthspan, the years you live in good health.
Salma reminds Omar of their mother, Layla, who broke her hip at seventy-nine. She lived for several more years, but she never again walked to the market or climbed the stairs alone.

In many countries, people spend several of their final years in poor health, although the numbers differ from place to place. Salma says a long-life plan tries to make that gap between the lines as short as possible.
Salma asks him to close his eyes and picture himself at eighty. Instead of asking how long he wants to live, she asks what he wants to be doing.
Omar takes out a notepad and writes down three wishes for himself at eighty. He wants to play on the floor with Lina's children, walk to the market, and see his father's village by the sea.
Salma turns each wish into a skill the body must have. Getting up from the floor needs strong legs, a long walk needs good stamina, and carrying a suitcase to the village needs strength.
Omar thinks of two of his neighbours, both of them seventy years old. One still gardens and cycles, while the other finds stairs hard, and Salma says that habits explain part of the difference.
Salma draws a line that slopes gently downward to show how our abilities fade with age. Fitter people start higher and reach the bottom later, so every bit of fitness built now is a kind of saving.
At home, Omar shows his list to Nadia, and she pins it to the fridge. Lina, who is climbing on the sofa, asks whether he will still be able to carry her when she is ten.

Late that night, Omar sits on the living-room floor and tries to stand up without using his hands. He needs both hands, a knee and a loud groan, and he decides that this will be his first small target.

On the April walk, Omar stops only three times, and Salma sketches four arrows on her notepad. They point to the four biggest threats: heart disease, cancer, type 2 diabetes and brain diseases such as dementia.

Heart disease usually begins when fatty deposits slowly narrow the arteries that carry blood. If a blockage stops the blood from reaching the heart, the result is a heart attack, as happened to Hamid.
Cancer is not one disease but many, and it begins when cells in the body grow out of control. Smoking, heavy drinking, extra weight, too little exercise and too much sun can all raise the risk.
In type 2 diabetes, the body stops handling sugar properly, so the level of sugar in the blood stays too high. Over many years this can damage the eyes, the nerves, the kidneys and the heart.
Dementia is the name for a group of brain diseases that harm memory, thinking and daily life. It becomes more common with age, and there is no sure way to prevent it, but some risks can be lowered.
Most of these diseases build up quietly over decades, long before anyone feels ill. That is why habits in your forties and fifties may matter more than they seem.
Salma takes a pack of cards from her pocket and fans out a hand on the bench. Genes and luck deal the cards, she says, but your habits decide how well you play them.

Omar remembers that their father, Karim, had a serious heart attack at sixty-one, and he asks whether he is doomed. Salma says that family history raises the risk, but it is a warning to act early and not a sentence.

Salma is honest about luck: some people who ignore their health live to ninety, and some who do everything right fall ill young. Nobody can promise a long life, but a good plan still improves the odds.
At the end of April, Hamid comes home and begins a rehabilitation programme, with exercise and advice from nurses. He tells Omar that his doctor said the heart attack was many years in the making.
At the May walk, Salma chalks four words on a flat stone beside the path. A fit body, she says, has four parts: stamina, strength, balance and flexibility.
Omar had always thought that being fit meant being able to run. Salma laughs: a keen runner may struggle to lift a heavy box, while someone who lifts heavy weights may puff on the stairs.
Stamina is the fitness of the heart and lungs, and it decides how long you can keep going. Omar, resting halfway up the steps with one hand on the rail, is learning exactly what his own stamina is.

In large studies, people with better stamina tend to live longer, and the link is one of the strongest that researchers have found. Salma adds that studies cannot prove cause, but improving at any age seems to help.

The World Health Organization advises adults to do at least 150 minutes of moderate activity each week, such as brisk walking. Going up to 300 minutes, or half that much hard exercise, brings extra benefits.
Salma teaches Omar a simple way to judge effort, which she calls the talk test. During moderate effort you breathe harder but can still talk, while during hard effort you manage only a few words.
Omar discovers that his usual stroll fails the test, because he could happily sing a song while he walks. When he follows Salma's brisk pace, he soon has to save his breath for the climb.
Omar decides to walk briskly for thirty minutes on five days a week, which makes 150 minutes. He will walk to school instead of taking the bus, and Nadia will join him on Sundays.
In the first week Omar's legs ache and he arrives at school with damp hair. By the third week, however, the walk has become easier, and he notices that he is sleeping a little better.
On a sunny Sunday in late May, Omar and Nadia walk fast along the river and still talk easily. For the first time, Omar feels that his stamina is really beginning to grow.
At the June walk, Salma explains that short bursts of hard effort can build fitness faster than steady walking alone. Researchers call this interval training, and it fits easily into a busy week.
Vigorous effort feels hard: your breathing is quick and deep, and you can say only a few words at a time. It should feel demanding, but never impossible, and you should recover within a few minutes.

Before they try anything hard, Salma raises a finger and looks quite serious. Anyone who is new to hard exercise, or who has a health condition, an injury or regular medicine, should ask a doctor before starting.
Dr Rahman, Omar's family doctor, listens to his chest and asks about his father's heart attack. She says that more exercise is a very good idea, as long as he builds up gradually.
Dr Rahman writes a short list on a card. Chest pain, fainting, dizziness, unusual breathlessness or sharp pain are all signs to stop at once and ask for medical help.

In the park, Omar tries his first intervals: one minute of very fast walking, then two minutes of slow walking, repeated four times. Lina rides beside him on her scooter and shouts that Grandpa is a rocket.
In the second week, Omar gets over-excited and does three hard sessions in four days. He feels exhausted and stiff, and Salma reminds him to start slowly and to add only a little each week.

Omar's thighs ache for two days after the session, and he wonders if something is wrong. Salma says dull, tired aching is normal after new exercise, but sharp pain, or pain that gets worse, means stop.
Salma draws a shape like a mountain on her notepad. Most of the week should be easy movement, with only one or two hard sessions, and rest days are when the body grows stronger.
By the end of June, Omar climbs the three flights to his flat without stopping. His pupils notice that he walks faster in the corridors, and one of them asks if he has joined a gym.
At the July walk, Salma puts her heavy rucksack on the path and lifts it with a straight back and bent knees. Strength, she says, is the second word on the stone, and the one most adults forget.
After about the age of thirty, most people slowly lose muscle unless they use it. The loss is gentle at first, but over several decades it can add up to a real problem.
Muscle is what lets us stand up from a chair, climb stairs and carry shopping home. Salma says that independence in old age is mostly made of ordinary movements like these.
Muscles also protect joints and bones, because they absorb shocks and hold the body steady. In addition, working muscle uses sugar from the blood, which helps to keep blood sugar healthy.

The World Health Organization advises muscle-strengthening activities on at least two days a week. Heavy bags, elastic bands, your own body weight or real weights all count, and a gym is not necessary.

Salma has brought a small grip tester, and she asks Omar to squeeze it as hard as he can. In large studies, weak grip strength has been linked with poorer health later in life, though it is only a clue.

Next, Omar stands up from a chair five times, without using his arms, while Salma times him. His results turn out to be average, which is neither shameful nor remarkable, and he feels strangely relieved.

Omar books a lesson with Leo, a qualified trainer at the Community Centre. Leo teaches him the basic movements, such as squatting, pushing and pulling, and says that good technique matters far more than heavy weights.
At home, Omar does squats from the kitchen chair, push-ups against the wall and rows with a rucksack full of books. Lina counts every repetition out loud, though she sometimes skips the number seven.
Hamid, with his doctor's approval and a nurse beside him, lifts light weights at his rehabilitation class. Both men add a little more each week, and neither of them is in a hurry.

Salma holds up a drawing of two bones, one thick and strong, the other thin and weak. Bones are living tissue, she says, and they grow stronger when they carry weight and are pulled by working muscles.
Calcium, vitamin D and protein all help to keep bones strong, and sunshine helps the body to make vitamin D. If bones become very weak, which is called osteoporosis, a doctor should look at them.

Salma tells Omar about Mr Ford, a patient who slipped on a wet kitchen floor and broke his wrist. Falls are one of the leading causes of injury in older people, she says, and many of them can be prevented.
Balance is a skill, and like every skill it improves with practice. Omar tries standing on one leg beside the kitchen counter, and he can only manage about five seconds before he wobbles.
On the way home, Omar watches a group doing tai chi in the park, moving as slowly as swimmers. Studies suggest that balance programmes, including tai chi, can reduce falls in older people.

Flexibility, the fourth word on the stone, means that the joints can move through their full range. Omar reaches toward his toes beside a park bench and finds that he can only get as far as his knees.
Gentle stretching and everyday movement, such as gardening, help the joints to stay supple. Omar makes a rule to play on the floor with Lina every day, getting down and up without help if he can.
On a hot afternoon in late July, Omar runs across the park after Lina's ball. His foot lands in a hole in the grass, his ankle twists, and he falls with a cry.
Omar's ankle swells up like a balloon, and Salma tells him to rest it and raise it on a cushion. Because he cannot put weight on it, he sees Dr Rahman, who judges it a bad sprain and not a break.

The August walk becomes a cup of tea at Rosa's Cafe, with Omar's bandaged foot on a spare chair. Salma says that setbacks happen to everyone, and that weak balance and weak ankles were part of the problem.
With his ankle in a bandage, Omar spends most of the day in an armchair. Salma phones to warn him that long periods of sitting are linked with poorer health.

Large studies link long hours of sitting with a higher risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes and early death. The risk seems greatest for people who exercise very little, and smaller for those who move a lot.

The advice is simple: break up long periods of sitting by standing or walking for a minute or two. Omar sets a kitchen timer to ring every half hour, and Lina takes great pleasure in making him obey it.
Salma shows Omar that he can still train the parts of his body that are not injured. Sitting in his chair, he lifts bags of rice and does arm and back exercises that put no weight on the ankle.
After three weeks the ankle is much better, and Dr Rahman says that Omar may start walking again. He begins with five minutes on flat ground, then ten, and he stops the moment it hurts.
Lina and her mother give Omar a simple step counter, tied with a big ribbon. Even with his short walks, he averages only about four thousand steps a day, far fewer than he expected.
In large studies, health benefits rise with daily steps and seem to level off at roughly seven to ten thousand. Even a few thousand extra steps a day can make a difference.
The famous number of ten thousand steps is not magic. It is widely said to come from an advertising slogan for a Japanese step counter sixty years ago, not from a study.
Omar finds easy ways to add steps: he walks while he is on the phone and takes the stairs, not the lift. Best of all, he and Nadia start a short walk after dinner every evening.
At the end of August, Omar finally climbs the steps of Bell Hill again. He is slower than in June and he stops twice, but Salma tells him that losing some ground after an injury is completely normal.
At the September walk, Salma says that we spend about a third of our lives asleep. Most adults need between seven and nine hours a night, and Omar, who sleeps about six, is suddenly interested.

Poor sleep is linked with heart disease, type 2 diabetes, low mood, accidents and poor memory. Many people who sleep too little say they feel fine, but tests often show that they do worse without knowing it.
The first habit of good sleep is regularity: going to bed and getting up at about the same time every day. Omar, a champion of sleeping late at weekends, receives this news with a heavy sigh.
A bedroom that is dark, quiet and cool helps most people to sleep better. Omar hangs thick curtains, covers the little red light on the television and opens the window a few centimetres.

Daylight in the morning helps to set the body's clock, so Omar takes his tea outside after breakfast. Caffeine late in the day, big evening meals and alcohol can all disturb sleep, even if alcohol makes you drowsy at first.
Bright screens late at night can make it harder to fall asleep, and the news on a phone is rarely calming. Omar agrees to charge his phone in the hallway, and he buys a cheap alarm clock.

Nadia admits that Omar snores loudly and that he sometimes seems to stop breathing for a few seconds. Salma says that loud snoring with pauses in breathing may be a sign of sleep apnoea, which a doctor can check.
Dr Rahman arranges a simple sleep test that Omar can do at home, with a small sensor on his finger. The result shows nothing worrying, and she explains that the snoring is probably just snoring.
Omar keeps a sleep diary for a month, writing down when he goes to bed, when he wakes and how he feels. After a few weeks he falls asleep faster, wakes before the alarm and needs far less coffee.
A short nap of twenty minutes can refresh the mind, but a long nap late in the day can make night sleep harder. Sleep, Salma says, is not a reward for finishing the plan, but a main part of it.

On the October walk, Salma begins by saying that she has no interest in strange diets. Eat mostly whole foods, she says, such as vegetables, fruit, beans, fish and whole grains, and less of the highly processed kind.

Large studies link diets rich in highly processed food, such as sweets, fizzy drinks and ready meals, with poorer health. It is hard to prove cause, but the pattern is consistent enough for Salma to give clear advice.
No single food is a miracle, and no single treat is a disaster. What matters is the pattern you keep for years, and Mediterranean-style eating has been linked with less heart disease.

Omar and Nadia change the way they shop in the supermarket on Saturday mornings. They read labels, choose beans, lentils, oats and frozen vegetables, and discover that eating well is often cheaper than eating badly.

Muscle is built from protein, and some experts suggest that older adults may need a little more of it than younger people. Eggs, fish, beans, yoghurt and lean meat are good sources, but people with kidney disease should ask a doctor first.
Fibre, which comes from vegetables, fruit, beans and whole grains, is good for the heart and for the gut. Omar sets himself a simple rule: at least one vegetable on his plate at every meal.
Sugary drinks add a great deal of sugar and almost nothing else, and many people forget to count them as food. Water, plain tea and coffee without much sugar are all better choices.
Magazines love miracle diets, but Salma has a simple test for any eating plan: could you follow it happily for ten years? Fasting patterns suit some people, and the evidence for them is still mixed.

Fat that collects deep inside the belly is linked with a higher risk of heart disease and type 2 diabetes. Salma measures Omar's waist with a soft tape, and says that a waist smaller than half your height is a rough guide.
Omar takes the result as information and not as an insult. Weight and waist are not the whole story, Salma says, so he sets a gentle goal: more movement, less sugar, one fewer biscuit.
On a cold November morning, Salma says that some of the most dangerous conditions give no warning at all. A few simple measurements, she says, can show them long before any symptoms appear.

High blood sugar over many years can damage the eyes, nerves, kidneys and heart, even when it causes no symptoms. A simple blood test can show whether the level is normal, and a doctor can explain the result.
A few days later, Omar goes to the clinic without breakfast, and a nurse takes a small sample of blood from his arm. He looks away, which she says is what most grown men do.
High blood pressure usually has no symptoms, but over the years it raises the risk of heart attack, stroke and kidney disease. The good news is that it is easy to measure and, if necessary, to treat.

At the clinic, Dr Rahman measures Omar's blood pressure twice, and the numbers are a little higher than she would like. She asks him to measure it at home for a week, sitting quietly, before she draws any conclusions.
Cholesterol is a fatty substance in the blood, and one kind, called LDL, can build up in the walls of the arteries. A blood test shows the level, and a doctor explains what it means for each person.

The results show that Omar's blood sugar is normal, but his LDL cholesterol is a little higher than ideal. Dr Rahman suggests changes to food and exercise, a new test in three months, and a look at his overall risk.

Omar measures his blood pressure every morning for a week, sitting quietly with a cup of tea. His readings at home are lower than at the clinic, which is common, because nervous patients often have higher numbers.
Salma warns that more tests are not always better. Some tests find harmless things and cause worry and more tests, so she tells Omar to ask his doctor what a result would change.
Omar writes his main numbers and test dates on a small card and slips it into his wallet. To know your numbers, Salma says, is not the same as to fear them.
Screening tests look for certain diseases before they cause any symptoms. Salma tells Omar that many countries invite people for them at set ages, and that the invitations are worth accepting.

Nadia has been invited for breast screening, which is offered to women in a certain age range in many countries. She goes to the appointment, it takes only a few minutes, and a week later the result is clear.
In some countries, people of Omar's age are invited to do a bowel screening test at home. A small kit arrives in the post; he makes a few jokes about it, and then he does the test and sends it off.

Other screening tests include cervical screening for women and checks of unusual moles on the skin. For some cancers, such as prostate cancer, experts disagree about routine testing, so it is a conversation to have with a doctor.

Screening, Salma explains, has both benefits and costs, like almost everything in medicine. No test is perfect, and false alarms happen, but for the main national programmes experts judge the benefits to be greater.
Mr Dalton, a teacher who smokes outside the school gate, asks Omar what has changed. Salma says that not smoking is one of the best things anyone can do, and that quitting helps at any age.

Salma explains that people who get support, such as a stop-smoking service or nicotine replacement, are much more likely to succeed. Many people need several attempts, and every attempt teaches something.

Health bodies agree that, with alcohol, less is better, although their advice on limits differs from country to country. Omar, who enjoys a glass of wine every evening, decides to have several alcohol-free days each week.
Not every risk comes from a slow disease, and some can be avoided with very little effort. Seat belts, cycle helmets, sun protection and working smoke alarms all prevent harm.

Recommended vaccines, such as those against flu, pneumonia and shingles, prevent serious illness in older adults, and each country has its own schedule. Omar asks Dr Rahman which ones he should have, and she checks his record.

On the December walk, Omar admits that the thing he fears most is losing his memory and forgetting Lina. Salma listens carefully and says that dementia is not a normal part of growing older, even though it becomes more common with age.

Everyone forgets keys or names now and then, and that alone is not dementia. If memory problems begin to interfere with daily life, or if family members become worried, it is sensible to see a doctor.

In 2024 an international group of experts reviewed the evidence and estimated that up to forty-five percent of dementia cases might be prevented or delayed. They found fourteen risk factors that people can sometimes do something about.
The first part of the list sounds familiar: high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes, smoking, alcohol and too little exercise. Extra weight and hearing loss are on the list too.

The rest of the list is surprising: head injuries, depression, loneliness, air pollution, poor eyesight and less time in school. Omar counts how many of the fourteen he can work on, and the answer is most of them.
Salma is careful about the limits of the evidence. The figure is only an estimate, and studies show links, not proof, but the steps are good for health anyway.
Omar books a hearing test at the local clinic. He presses a button whenever he hears a tone, and the test shows a mild loss of the highest sounds.

Untreated hearing loss is linked with a higher risk of dementia, perhaps because the brain works harder or because people withdraw from company. Whether hearing aids can lower the risk is still being studied, but they certainly help people to join in.
Poor eyesight is linked with falls and dementia, and many eye problems can be treated if found early. Omar has an eye test, and the optician tells him that he needs reading glasses.

At the top of the hill, Salma says that the body and the brain are not two separate projects. Whatever helps the heart, the lungs and the muscles usually helps the mind, and next she wants to talk about learning.
Omar has always wanted to play the guitar, so he dusts off his old one and signs up for lessons at the Community Centre. His teacher is a patient young man called Teo.
At the first lesson Omar's fingertips burn, and every chord he plays buzzes like an angry bee. Teo only smiles and says that every player in the world began exactly like this.
On the January walk, Omar proudly tells Salma about his guitar lessons. She says people who keep learning tend to have a lower dementia risk, though this is a link, not proof.
Omar mentions a brain-training app that he has downloaded on his phone. Salma explains that these games make people better at the games, but there is little evidence that this helps everyday memory.

Salma says that good learning has three parts: it is new, it is hard, and it is regular. Ten minutes every day beats an hour once a month, because short, regular practice is what helps a skill to stick.
At home Lina climbs onto Omar's lap and plucks the strings with great seriousness. She announces that she wants a song, so he practises a simple tune for a whole week.
Halfway up the hill, Omar and Salma meet Mrs Hale, who is eighty-three. She climbs Bell Hill with a stick two mornings a week, and she refuses to be hurried.
Mrs Hale tells them that she looks after a small street garden near the bottom of the hill. She only began growing vegetables at seventy-five, she says, and she wishes she had started sooner.
Omar offers to dig a bed and soon feels warm and pleasantly dirty. Salma says that gardening mixes gentle movement, fresh air and daylight, and that heavy digging can count as muscle work.

At the top of the hill, Omar takes out his guitar and plays his tune, with only two mistakes. Salma claps and says that it is the doing, not the cleverness, that matters, so he should keep on learning.
Salma says that long-lasting loneliness is linked with a higher risk of early death, heart disease and dementia. As always, she reminds Omar that a link is a warning and not a proof.
Omar visits Hamid, who now walks every morning and looks much healthier. Hamid says that the best part of his rehabilitation group was the other patients, who understood exactly how he felt.
Scrolling through his phone, Omar sees the name of Yusuf, an old friend. They have not spoken for two years, and Omar cannot even remember why.
The first minute of the call is awkward, and both men apologise. After that the years fall away, and they promise to climb Bell Hill together on Saturday.
Salma tells Omar that close relationships are linked with better health and a longer life. Friends help each other to stay active, and they notice when something is wrong.
At the bottom of the hill, Omar meets Mr Okafor, who is seventy-one and leads a walking group. The Tuesday Walkers climb Bell Hill every week, whatever the weather.
Omar joins the Tuesday Walkers and finds that he walks faster than usual without noticing. Studies suggest that people keep exercising for longer when they do it with others.
After each walk, the group meets at Rosa's Cafe for tea and toast. A quiet widower tells Omar that the group is the reason he leaves his house in winter.
Salma says that quality matters more than numbers, and that a few close friends are enough. A call, a message or a shared meal is often all it takes to keep a friendship alive.
Omar asks Nadia to cook for his new and old friends, and she is delighted. Hamid, Samira, Yusuf, Mr Okafor and Salma crowd around the table, and the flat is full of noise.
Hill Road School is waiting for an inspection, and Omar is working late and sleeping badly. Salma says that a little stress is normal, and in short bursts it can even help.
Salma explains that stress which lasts for weeks is linked with poor sleep, low mood and higher blood pressure. It also pushes many people towards late snacks, extra coffee and skipped walks.
Salma says that nobody can remove all stress from life. What helps is recovery, and exercise, time outdoors, friends and good sleep all assist it.
Salma shows Omar how to breathe slowly, with a longer breath out than in. Some studies suggest this can help people to feel calmer, although the evidence is modest.
On a short lunch break, Omar walks around a green park near the school. Time in green places is linked with a better mood, and he feels his shoulders drop.
Samira tells Omar that Hamid has been low and quiet lately, and she is worried. Salma says that low mood is common after a heart attack and that Hamid should tell his doctor.
Omar visits Hamid but does not try to fix anything. He listens, and later they walk slowly to the corner of the street and back.
Salma says that low mood on most days for two weeks or more is worth telling a doctor about. Hamid does, and his doctor arranges support and regular check-ins.
Salma says that people with a strong sense of purpose tend to live longer and in better health. The link probably works both ways, since healthy people can pursue their goals more easily.
Omar asks himself what his purpose is, and the answer comes quickly: teaching, family and friends. He starts a Thursday walking club at Hill Road School for pupils and staff.
On the February walk, Omar admits that he feels overwhelmed. There are so many good habits on the list that he does not know how anyone could keep them all going.
Salma says that people who try to change everything at once usually fail. It is much better to change one or two things, and let them settle before adding more.
Salma suggests that Omar keep a small notebook with one line for each day. He writes whether he walked, whether he lifted something heavy and how well he slept.
Writing things down shows progress and keeps people honest. Salma warns that numbers are guides and not judges, and that worrying about every figure helps nobody.
Salma tells him to link a new habit to an old one that he already does without thinking. Omar decides to stand on one leg every time he waits for the kettle to boil.
Salma says that good habits should be small and easy. Omar puts his trainers beside the front door and starts with just two minutes, because getting started is the hardest part.
Nadia, who has read about habits at the library, says that a new habit takes time to feel automatic. One well-known study found that it took about two months on average, but people varied widely.
One evening Omar is too tired and misses his walk. Salma says that one missed day does no harm, but it is wise to get back on track the next day.
Soon the whole family joins in, and Nadia starts her own notebook. Lina puts a gold star on the fridge calendar for every day that her grandfather moves.
Omar repeats his two tests, and he stands up from a chair five times much faster. He also balances on one leg for about twenty seconds, instead of only five in the summer.
In the staff room, a colleague shows Omar an advertisement for an anti-ageing pill that costs as much as a month's rent. Omar sends a photo of it to Salma and asks if it works.
That evening Salma tells Omar that no supplement or medicine has so far been proved to slow ageing in people. Many claims rest on studies of cells or animals, which are a long way from real life.

Salma says that some supplements are useful, because a doctor may find that a person really lacks something. A lack of vitamin D is one example, but supplements can clash with medicines, so ask first.

Salma teaches Omar how to recognise the main warning signs of hype. Be careful with words like miracle and secret, with stories instead of studies, and with one expensive product that promises quick results.

Salma says that real scientists do study ageing, and they take it seriously. They work with worms, flies and mice, and some medicines used for other illnesses are being tested to see if they help people.
Salma explains that results in animals often fail in people. A mouse lives about two years and a person lives for many decades, and a clean laboratory is nothing like real life.
Omar adds up the cost of his whole plan. He needs walking shoes, a rucksack of books, beans, oats and a good night's sleep, and the total is almost nothing.
Mr Dalton, the colleague who smoked, joins a free stop-smoking service and finally quits. He has saved a good sum of money, and he says that his morning cough is much better.
Salma says that money can help with real needs, such as glasses, hearing aids or a blood pressure monitor. It cannot buy fitness, because fitness has to be earned slowly, a day at a time.
On the cover of his notebook Omar writes that health is earned and not bought. The best investment, he decides, is not money but time, spent a little every day.
In the last grey weeks of winter, Omar catches a heavy cold that turns into flu. He stays in bed for several days and misses school, his walks and his guitar lesson.
Even after his fever has gone, Omar does almost nothing for ten days. He feels flat and guilty, and the habits that he worked so hard to build begin to slip away.
Salma visits Omar, and to his surprise she does not give a lecture. She says that setbacks are part of every plan, so a good plan always includes a way to restart.
Salma gives Omar a common rule of thumb for starting again after an illness. With mild symptoms above the neck, light exercise is usually fine, but with a fever or chest symptoms, rest.
Omar restarts at about half his old level, with a slow ten-minute walk on the flat. He is surprised at how breathless he is, but he does not give up.
Within two weeks Omar is almost back at his usual level of walking. Salma says that fitness lost during a short break often returns quickly, though it takes longer after a long one.

At the Community Centre, Omar meets Iris, who uses a wheelchair and lifts weights three times a week. Salma says that almost everyone can find a way to train, and that even people in their eighties and nineties can gain strength.
Salma says that each stage of life has its own priorities. In the thirties and forties, build habits; in the fifties and sixties, protect muscle and bone; later, keep balance and independence.
The dark weeks pass, and the mornings grow lighter. Omar feels his mood lift as he walks in the morning light, and Nadia notices that he is humming again.
In Mrs Hale's street garden, the first snowdrops are pushing through the soil. Omar sends Salma a message to book the last walk of the year, and he feels ready.
A year has passed, and it is March again, two weeks after Omar's fifty-third birthday. Omar stands with Salma at the bottom of Bell Hill, looking up at the same one hundred and sixty steps.
Omar starts to climb at a steady pace, counting each step in his head. Salma, who usually has a great deal to say, follows quietly and lets him lead the way.
Omar reaches the bench where he stopped four times a year ago, and he walks straight past it. Salma, watching his back, smiles to herself and says nothing.
Omar reaches the top of the hill without having to stop even once. He is breathing hard, but he can still speak in full sentences, which means that he passes the talk test.
To end the climb, Salma asks Omar to sit on the grass and get up again without using his hands. He does it, wobbling slightly, and he laughs out loud with delight.
Omar asks how many extra years he has gained, but Salma says that nobody can tell him. No plan can promise a long life, but a good plan improves the odds and the quality of the years.
Omar counts what he has gained on his fingers: stairs without stopping, the floor, better sleep, new friends and a guitar tune. He is surprised at how long the list is.
Salma takes out a pen and writes the whole plan on a single sheet of paper. It has six short lines: move, lift, sleep, eat well, keep friends close and have regular check-ups.
The whole family and many friends arrive at the top for a picnic, including Hamid, who has climbed every step. Omar plays his guitar, and Lina asks him if he will carry her when she is ten.
Omar's plan went on the fridge beside Lina's gold stars, and there it stayed. This book is general information and is not medical advice, so please ask a doctor about your own health.
C1C2: On the first Saturday of March, Omar turned fifty-two, and his small flat filled with the noise and warmth of a family birthday. His wife Nadia had baked a lemon cake, his daughter Dina had brought balloons, and his granddaughter Lina, who was five, insisted on blowing out every candle on his behalf. Omar, a teacher with a comfortable stomach and a friendly manner, laughed along with everyone, never suspecting how soon the evening would change his mind about a few things.

Just as the cake was being cut, Omar's phone buzzed in his pocket, and he stepped into the hallway to answer it. The voice on the line belonged to Hamid's wife, Samira, and she told him, in a thin and careful tone, that her husband had suffered a heart attack that afternoon. Hamid, Omar's closest friend since their schooldays, was only fifty-three, and until that moment Omar had always considered him the sturdy one of the two.

The next morning Omar sat beside Hamid's hospital bed, surrounded by the soft beeping of monitors and the smell of disinfectant. His friend looked smaller than he remembered, pale against the white pillow, and he admitted that he had never imagined such a thing could happen to him. “I felt fine the day before,” Hamid whispered, and Omar had no answer, because he knew that he would have said exactly the same.

That evening, as Omar climbed the three flights to his flat, he was obliged to pause on the landing with one hand on the cold rail and his chest heaving. It struck him with uncomfortable force that he had not exercised in years, that he drove everywhere, and that he had never once asked himself where his habits were leading. Hamid's arteries had been narrowing quietly for a long time, and Omar began to wonder what might be happening, just as quietly, inside him.

Long after midnight, with two cold cups of tea between them, Nadia told her husband that worrying was not a plan and that he ought to do something about it. She reminded him, with the gentle firmness of thirty years of marriage, that his younger sister Salma was a physiotherapist who spent every working day with people whose bodies had stopped cooperating. Omar had always found Salma slightly intimidating, but he picked up the phone before he could change his mind.

Salma arrived the next afternoon with a rucksack on her back and a flask of tea in her hand, and she listened to her brother's story without interrupting once. When he had finished, she warned him that she had no magic to offer and no secret to sell, since she had long ago lost patience with the miracle cures that fill the internet and the shops. What she did have, she said, was a good understanding of the evidence, and a stubborn habit of telling people exactly how sure she was.

Salma unfolded a map on the kitchen table and tapped a small green circle on the edge of town, which was Bell Hill, famous for its long flight of stone steps. Her proposal was a bargain: they would climb it together once a month for a year, from one birthday to the next, and each time she would answer one question as truthfully as the evidence allowed. There would be no hype, no promises and no miracles, only what is known, how well it is known, and what a sensible person might do about it.

Two weeks after the birthday, on a cool grey Saturday, Omar stood at the bottom of Bell Hill and looked up at the stone steps climbing away from him between the trees. There were one hundred and sixty of them, worn smooth in the middle by generations of feet, and the last few seemed to disappear into the mist. Salma, who had already tied her laces and was bouncing lightly on her toes, told him that the hill would be patient with him and that he should try to be patient with it.

Omar climbed with great determination for the first forty steps and then with great misery for the rest, stopping four times with his hands on his knees and his lungs working like a pair of old bellows. Salma waited each time without comment, her eyes on the valley rather than on his red face, which he found remarkably kind of her. At the top she told him that there was no shame in any of it, since a starting point is only a place from which to measure the journey.

At the top, as the town lay spread out below them like a model of itself, they shared the tea from Salma's flask while Omar's heart slowly stopped hammering. Before they walked down, she told him that the first question of the year would be hers rather than his, and that it was this: what exactly is a long life for? He promised to think about it, and found, to his surprise, that he was already looking forward to the next walk.

On the back of the map, Salma drew two horizontal lines, one longer than the other, and labelled them with the two words that would shape the whole year. The long line was lifespan, the number of years a person lives, while the short line was healthspan, the number of those years lived in good health, free from serious illness or disability. Everyone talks about the first, she said, but it is the second that decides whether the extra years are a gift or a burden.

Salma points out that their own mother, Layla, was a living example of the gap between the two lines. Layla broke her hip at seventy-nine and lived for several more years, but she never again walked to the market, climbed the stairs or travelled alone, and those years were smaller than the ones before. Omar remembered sitting with her by the window, thinking that she was not sick so much as shut in.

In many countries, studies suggest, people spend several of their last years living with illness or disability, though the figures vary a great deal from place to place. Salma runs her finger along the gap between the two lines and says that it is the real target of everything they will talk about this year. A plan that added years but not health, she adds, would be only half a success, and not the half that anyone would choose.

Salma invites her brother to close his eyes and imagine himself at eighty, not as a number on a birthday card but as a person doing particular things. She explains that the most useful planning works backwards from a picture of a good old age, rather than forwards from a vague hope of living long. Omar sits on the bench with his eyes shut for a full minute, and when he opens them, they are slightly wet.

Omar took out a notepad and, after some thought, wrote down three wishes for the old man he hoped to become. He wanted to sit on the floor with Lina's children and get up again without help, to walk to the market every morning with a bag of oranges, and to visit the seaside village where his father had been born. They were modest wishes, he noticed, and every one of them would ask something definite of his body.

Salma took the pencil and drew an arrow from each wish to the physical ability that lay behind it. Sitting on the floor and rising again needed strength and balance, a morning walk needed stamina, and a trip to the village meant carrying a suitcase and climbing stairs. Abilities are spent slowly, like money from a bank account, and it is far easier to save them now than to borrow them back at seventy-nine.

Omar thought of two neighbours, both seventy years old, whose lives could hardly differ more: one still gardened and cycled to the shops, while the other struggled with the stairs and rarely left his chair. Habits explain part of that difference, Salma said, but luck, genes and illness explain the rest, and nobody should be blamed for what life has handed them. What the evidence does show is that the habits are the part a person can still change.

On the notepad Salma drew a line that sloped gently downward, to show how strength, stamina and balance all fade slowly with the years. A person who builds fitness now, she explained, starts higher on the line and takes much longer to reach the point where ordinary life becomes difficult, so that fitness behaves like savings in the bank. The line cannot be made to rise forever, but it can be lifted, and a gentler slope is worth almost as much as a higher start.

At home that evening, Omar showed his list to Nadia, who read it twice, smiled in a way that he could not quite interpret, and pinned it to the refrigerator with a magnet shaped like a lemon. Lina, who was bouncing on the sofa behind them, asked whether Grandpa would still be strong enough to carry her when she was ten years old. He said yes without hesitating, and then lay awake wondering whether it was a promise he had the right to make.

Unable to sleep, Omar crept into the living room, sat down cross-legged on the carpet and tried to stand up again without using his hands. It took both hands, one knee and a groan loud enough to make him freeze in case he woke the whole building, and he sank back onto the sofa feeling oddly humbled. It was not a disaster, but it was information, and as Salma had promised, information was where every sensible plan began.

Omar arrived for the April walk with slightly less dread, and he reached the top having stopped only three times. There, Salma drew four arrows on her notepad and named the four great threats to a long and healthy life: diseases of the heart and blood vessels, cancer, type 2 diabetes, and brain diseases such as dementia. Between them, she said, these account for a very large share of the illness and early death in wealthy countries, and each one deserves a closer look.

Heart disease, Salma explains, usually begins quietly, as fatty deposits build up inside the arteries and narrow the passage through which blood must flow. In time a deposit may crack or a clot may form on top of it, the blood is cut off from part of the heart muscle, and the result is a heart attack. That, she says gently, is very probably what happened to Hamid, though only his doctors can know the details.

Cancer, Salma tells him, is not a single disease but a large family of them, each beginning when cells in some part of the body start to divide out of control.
