Some of the causes are beyond anyone's power, but smoking, heavy drinking, extra body fat, a lack of exercise and too much sun are known to raise the risk of several kinds. Other cancers can be found early by screening, which is a good reason to learn what tests are on offer.

In type 2 diabetes, the body gradually becomes worse at managing the sugar in the blood, and the level stays higher than it should. Extra weight, little exercise and a poor diet all raise the risk, though genes play a part too, and the damage to the eyes, nerves, kidneys and heart often accumulates silently for years. The encouraging news, Salma adds, is that for many people the condition can be prevented or delayed, and sometimes improved, by changes in everyday habits.

Dementia, Salma says, is not one illness but a group of them, in which the brain slowly loses the ability to remember, reason and manage ordinary daily life. Alzheimer's disease is the most common form, it becomes more frequent as people grow older, and at present nobody has a certain way to prevent it. Yet some of the things that raise the risk are within a person's reach, and she promises that they will come back to those later in the year.

Salma points to a sapling and an ancient oak beside the path and says that a disease, like a tree, spends most of its life underground, growing silently long before anyone sees it. A narrowed artery, a loss of muscle or a rise in blood sugar may begin decades before the first symptom, and by the time a problem announces itself, the choices are fewer. For that reason, the unglamorous habits of the forties and fifties may be among the best investments a person can make.

From her pocket Salma produced a pack of cards and fanned a hand of them out on the bench between the two tea mugs. Genes and luck deal the cards, she said, and nobody gets to choose what they are handed, but the way a person plays the hand can change the odds a great deal. A good player with poor cards often beats a careless one with excellent ones, although, as every gambler knows, nothing is guaranteed.

Omar admits that what really frightens him is his father, Karim, who had a serious heart attack at sixty-one and lived with heart disease for the next fifteen years, and he asks whether he is already doomed. Salma shakes her head firmly and explains that a family history raises the risk without settling the outcome, and that it is best understood as an early warning. People who know their family history can ask their doctors to check them sooner and more carefully, which is a real advantage, since it allows problems to be caught early.

Salma is careful to be honest about luck, because she has met people who ignored every piece of advice and lived to ninety, and others who did everything right and fell ill in their forties. Individual stories like these are vivid, she says, but they tell us almost nothing about the odds, which only become visible when thousands of people are counted. A good plan does not buy a guarantee; it buys a better chance, and a better chance, repeated over a lifetime, is worth having.

Towards the end of April, Hamid came home from hospital with a bag of tablets and a place on a rehabilitation programme, where nurses and physiotherapists would supervise his exercise and teach him how to look after his heart. He told Omar, with a wry smile, that his doctor had described the heart attack as the last act of a play that had been running for many years. Omar felt a cold prickle on the back of his neck, because he realised that his own play might already be well into its second act.

On the third walk, in the first week of May, Salma stopped beside a flat stone near the path and chalked four words on it in her neat capitals. Being fit, she explained, is not one thing but four: stamina, strength, balance and flexibility, and a person can be excellent at one while being hopeless at the others. Most people, she added with a sideways look, have chosen their favourite and quietly ignored the rest.

Omar confesses that he had always imagined fitness to mean running, a pastime he had abandoned at about the age of nineteen. Salma laughs and tells him that a keen runner may struggle to lift a heavy box or stand on one leg, while a champion weightlifter can be left gasping by a flight of stairs. Real fitness, she says, is a balanced collection of abilities, and the ones that people neglect are often the ones they later need most.

Stamina, Salma says, is the fitness of the heart, lungs and blood vessels working together, and it decides how long a person can keep moving before the body demands a rest. Omar, who had paused halfway up the steps with one hand on the iron rail and an expression of deep concentration, was receiving a practical lesson in what his own stamina amounted to. Every extra step he could take without stopping, she observed cheerfully, would be a small but measurable improvement.

In large studies that followed people for many years, those with higher stamina tended to live longer than those with less, and Salma says that this link is one of the strongest that researchers have found. She is careful to add that such studies show an association rather than a proof, since fitter people may differ from others in other ways as well. Even so, she says, the pattern is so consistent, and the cost of acting on it so low, that she is quite happy to base advice on it.

The World Health Organization advises adults to aim for at least 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity every week, such as brisk walking, or half that amount of vigorous activity such as running. Salma points out that this works out at about half an hour on most days, which is less than the time many people spend choosing something to watch in the evening. Anything is better than nothing, she insists, and in general the benefits keep growing as the total rises, although the largest gains come to those who move from none to some.

To judge how hard he is working without any gadgets, Omar learns the talk test, which Salma recommends to all her patients. During moderate effort a person breathes harder than usual but can still hold a conversation, while during vigorous effort only a few words can be managed before another breath is needed. It is a rough guide rather than a laboratory measurement, she admits, but it has the great advantages of being free and impossible to lose.

Omar discovers, rather to his embarrassment, that his usual stroll fails the test completely, since he could sing an entire song on the way to the bakery without missing a note. When he tries to keep up with Salma's brisk pace along the lane, the situation changes at once: his breathing deepens, his face grows warm, and he can manage only short sentences. That, she tells him, is what moderate effort feels like, and it is the effort that counts towards the weekly total.

Back at home, Omar turned the idea into a schedule, which pleased the teacher in him: thirty minutes of brisk walking on five days of the week, adding up to the 150 minutes that the experts recommend. He would leave the car at home and walk to Hill Road School in the mornings, while Nadia, who had long wanted an excuse to see more of the neighbourhood, agreed to join him for a longer stroll on Sundays. It was not a heroic plan, and that, Salma had told him, was precisely why it might work.

In the first week, his calves ached, his shoes rubbed and he arrived at school looking as though he had been rescued from a river. By the third week, however, the damp hair had become a badge of honour, the walk had become easier, and he noticed that he was sleeping more deeply and thinking more clearly before the first lesson. Hill Road School, he reflected, had never had a teacher who arrived so cheerful, or so thoroughly out of breath.

On a bright Sunday at the end of May, Omar and Nadia walked briskly along the river, passing the talk test with ease and several dog-walkers with something close to arrogance. For the first time in years, Omar felt his body responding to what he asked of it, and the sensation was less like effort than like a door quietly opening. Nadia, who had begun the walk with doubts, remarked that he had stopped whistling and started telling stories, which she took to be a good sign.

At the June walk, which the warm weather had turned into something close to a picnic, Salma explained that short bursts of hard effort can raise fitness faster, minute for minute, than steady walking alone. Researchers call this interval training, and the idea is to alternate a minute or two of demanding effort with a longer period of easy recovery. Because it takes so little time, she added, it suits people whose main excuse is that they are busy.

Vigorous effort, Salma says, is the kind that makes the breathing quick and deep, the legs heavy and the conversation brief, so that a person can manage only a few words before gasping for air. It should feel demanding without ever becoming unbearable, and a sensible rule is to stop as soon as the effort feels out of control. Omar, who has never in his adult life deliberately made himself breathless, listens with a mixture of curiosity and dread.

Before they try anything hard, Salma raises a finger and puts on her most serious expression. Anyone new to vigorous exercise, she says, or with a health condition, an injury or regular medication, should ask a doctor first, since the right advice depends on the person and she cannot give it from a hilltop. Omar, who is fifty-two and has not been checked for years, promises to book an appointment that same week.

Dr Rahman, who had looked after Omar's family for fifteen years, listened to his chest, checked his pulse and asked a series of questions about his father's heart attack and about what his own days were like. She told him that more exercise was a very good idea, particularly given his family history, but that he should build up gradually and keep her informed. Her only real worry, she said with a twinkle, was that he had waited so long to ask.

Before he left, Dr Rahman wrote a short list on a card and made him read it aloud. Chest pain, fainting, dizziness, unusual breathlessness and sudden sharp pain, she said, are all signs to stop immediately and seek medical advice, and to call an emergency number if they do not pass. Omar tucked the card into his wallet behind a photograph of Lina, where he hoped it would stay unread for a very long time.

On a Saturday morning in the park, Omar tried his first intervals: one minute of very fast walking, then two minutes of easy strolling to recover, the whole pattern repeated four times. Lina rode alongside on her scooter, timing him with a toy stopwatch and announcing to the astonished dog-walkers that her grandfather was a rocket. By the fourth effort his legs were trembling, his heart was drumming, and he felt, absurdly, entirely alive.

In the second week Omar, intoxicated by his own progress, crammed three hard sessions into four days and ended the week exhausted, stiff and unusually bad-tempered. Salma, when she heard about it, was not surprised, and she reminded him that most injuries happen to people who try to make up for decades of inactivity in a fortnight. The rule, she said, is to start slowly and to add a little each week, and the body will repay the patience with interest.

For two days after his hardest session, Omar's thighs ached so badly that he descended the stairs backwards, and he rang Salma to ask whether something was wrong. She laughed kindly and explained that a dull, heavy, tired ache in the muscles, peaking a day or two after unfamiliar exercise, is perfectly normal and usually harmless. A sudden sharp pain, a joint that swells, or any pain that grows worse instead of better, she added, is a different matter and deserves a professional opinion.

On her notepad Salma drew a mountain with a broad base and a small, sharp peak, and she explained that training should look the same. Most of the week should be easy or moderate movement, with perhaps one or two hard sessions at the top, because the body improves not during the effort but during the recovery that follows it. Sleep, food and rest days are therefore part of the training and not a reward for it.

By the end of June, Omar could climb the three flights of stairs to his flat without stopping, a feat that would have seemed impossible on the evening of Hamid's heart attack. At school, his pupils noticed that he strode along the corridors with a new briskness, and one cheeky boy asked whether he had joined a gym or been replaced by a younger teacher. Omar, who had never felt more pleased with a compliment, told him that the secret was a hill, a sister and a great deal of tea.

At the July walk, in air as warm as bathwater, Salma set her heavy rucksack on the path and showed Omar how to lift it properly, with a straight back, bent knees and the load held close to her body. Strength, she said, was the second word on the stone, and it was the one that most adults abandoned somewhere around their twenties and never thought about again. Omar lifted the rucksack, grunted, and admitted that it was heavier than it looked.

From about the age of thirty, Salma explains, most people begin to lose muscle very slowly, and the loss continues for the rest of life unless the muscles are given a reason to stay. At first the change is too gentle to notice, but over several decades it can add up to the difference between a body that carries its own shopping and one that needs help with the stairs. The encouraging part is that muscle responds to training at almost any age, even in the nineties.

Muscle, Salma says, is not about appearance but about independence, because it is what allows a person to rise from a chair, climb stairs, carry shopping home and get up from the floor after a fall. She has treated patients who were mentally sharp and entirely willing to live alone, but whose legs simply could no longer lift them from the sofa. Independence in old age, she concludes, is mostly made of ordinary movements, and strong muscles are what pay for them.

Strong muscles protect the joints and bones that they surround, Salma continues, by absorbing shocks and holding the body steady when it twists or stumbles. They also play a quiet part in metabolism, since working muscle takes sugar out of the blood, which is one reason why strength training can help with blood sugar control. In other words, she says, the muscles are not only the engine of the body but also a kind of storage room for fuel.

The World Health Organization advises adults to do muscle-strengthening activities on at least two days of each week, working all the major muscle groups of the legs, hips, back, chest, shoulders and arms. Salma points out that what matters is a muscle meeting resistance, so that a heavy bag, an elastic band, a child on the shoulders or the weight of the body itself will all do the job. A gym is pleasant for those who enjoy one, and a good teacher is a gift, but a person can build real strength in a spare room.

To give him a starting point, Salma has brought a small grip tester from her clinic, and she asks Omar to squeeze it as hard as he possibly can while she writes down the number. In large studies weak grip strength has been linked with poorer health and a higher risk of early death, although it is a clue rather than a diagnosis, and it can be improved with training. Omar squeezes with his whole face, which she assures him does not add to the score.

Then she makes him stand up from a chair five times in a row with his arms crossed over his chest, while she times him with her watch and tries to look neutral. His numbers turn out to be average, which is neither shameful nor remarkable, and to his own surprise he feels strangely relieved to know exactly where he stands. Tests like these, she reminds him, are only clues, and what matters far more is the direction in which the numbers move.

On Salma's advice, Omar books a lesson with Leo, a qualified trainer at the Community Centre, a cheerful young man with forearms like loaves of bread. Leo teaches him the basic movements one at a time, the squat, the hinge at the hips, the push and the pull, and insists that good technique matters far more than the weight on the bar. By the end of the hour, Omar has been told to stop looking at the mirror and to start looking at his knees.

At home, with no equipment but a kitchen chair, a wall and a rucksack filled with old textbooks, Omar works through a short routine of squats, push-ups against the wall and pulling movements with the bag. Lina appoints herself the official counter and announces each repetition at the top of her voice, although she has a persistent tendency to skip the number seven. Twenty minutes later he is damp, pleased and, in a way he cannot quite explain, a little proud of his textbooks.

Hamid, with his doctor's approval and a nurse at his elbow, was lifting light weights at his rehabilitation class, and he called Omar every Friday to compare their progress like two schoolboys swapping football cards. Both men added a little more each week, a single extra repetition or a slightly heavier bag, and both discovered that patience is itself a kind of strength. By the middle of July, Omar could do ten squats without wobbling and Hamid could carry his own shopping.

Further up the hill, Salma holds up a drawing of two bones, one thick and dense, the other thin and fragile, and explains that bone is living tissue that responds to the demands made on it. Walking, climbing and lifting all send small forces through the skeleton, and the bones answer by becoming stronger, which is why astronauts, who float, lose bone so quickly. A skeleton, she adds, is not a coat hanger but a building in constant repair.

Calcium, vitamin D and protein all help to build and keep strong bones, Salma says, and the body makes its own vitamin D when the skin is touched by sunlight, though in northern winters many people fall short. When bones become very weak and break easily, the condition is called osteoporosis, and it is a matter for a doctor, who may suggest a bone scan, medicine or changes to the diet. For most people, she adds, the first line of defence is the same as for muscles: carry some weight, and carry it often.

Salma tells Omar about Mr Ford, a patient of eighty who slipped on a wet kitchen floor, broke his wrist and needed months to recover his confidence as well as his grip. Falls, she says, are one of the leading causes of injury in older people, and the consequences, from broken hips to a fear of going out, can reshape an entire life. The reassuring fact is that many falls can be prevented, and the best prevention begins long before anyone is old.

Balance, Salma insists, is a skill, and like any skill it improves with practice and fades without it. That evening Omar stood on one leg beside the kitchen counter, with a hand hovering close to it for safety, and discovered that he could hold the position for about five seconds before his foot began to dance. His left leg was a little better than his right, and the whole business was more humbling than he would have predicted.

On the way home from the hill, Omar stopped to watch a group of people practising tai chi on the grass, moving as slowly and gracefully as swimmers in a dream. Salma, who had joined him at the railing, explained that exercise programmes aimed at balance, tai chi among them, have been shown in trials to reduce falls in older people. It looked so effortless that Omar was rather startled when the teacher, a woman of seventy-six, invited him to try.

Flexibility, the fourth word on the stone, means that the joints can still move through their full range, so that a person can reach a high shelf, tie a shoelace or look over a shoulder when reversing a car. Beside a park bench, Omar bends forward to touch his toes and discovers, after a determined effort, that his fingertips can reach no lower than his knees. Salma assures him that this is exactly where most men of his age begin, and that the toes will not run away.

Gentle stretching, held for half a minute without bouncing, and the ordinary movements of life, such as gardening, sweeping and playing on the floor, all help the joints to stay supple. Omar makes it a rule to sit on the carpet with Lina every evening and to get up again with as little help from his hands as possible, a project that she regards as the best game ever invented. By the end of the week he can manage it with one hand, and the groaning has dropped to a polite murmur.

On a hot afternoon in late July, Omar, feeling pleasantly invincible after a month of training, sprinted across the park to rescue Lina's runaway ball. His left foot came down in a hidden hole in the grass, his ankle folded sideways with a sickening click, and he collapsed with a shout that sent the pigeons flapping into the trees. Lina stood perfectly still, her eyes enormous, and then said very quietly that she was sorry about the ball.

By evening the ankle had swollen to the size of a grapefruit, and Salma, who arrived within the hour, told him to rest it, raise it on a cushion and protect it from any weight. Because he could not put any weight on it, he saw Dr Rahman the next morning, who examined it carefully and judged it a bad sprain rather than a break. She prescribed rest, a firm bandage and patience, in that order, and warned him that patience would be the hardest.

The August walk became nothing more than a cup of tea at Rosa's Cafe at the foot of Bell Hill, with Omar's bandaged foot propped on a spare chair and the stone steps staring down at him like a reproach. Salma told him that setbacks happen to everyone who tries to change, and that weak balance and unprepared ankles had probably played a part in his fall. What mattered now, she said, was not the injury itself but how sensibly he behaved while it healed.

With his ankle in a bandage and his schoolwork spread around him, Omar spent most of the first week in the same armchair, rising only for meals and the bathroom. Salma telephoned on the fifth day, having guessed exactly what was happening, to warn him that long unbroken periods of sitting are linked with poorer health. She added that there was a certain irony in a man who had just learned to walk becoming a champion sitter.

Large studies, Salma explains, link long hours of sitting with a higher risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes and early death, even after allowing for other differences between people. The risk appears greatest for those who also take very little exercise, and smaller for those who move a great deal, although nobody can yet say exactly how many hours of sitting are too many. For the moment, the sensible rule is to treat every chair as a place for resting and not as a place for living.

The advice, Salma says, is refreshingly simple: interrupt long periods of sitting every half hour or so with a minute or two of standing, stretching or walking around the room. Omar sets a kitchen timer to ring on the hour and the half hour, and when Lina visits, she appoints herself its enforcer, marching him around the flat with the solemnity of a prison guard. Even the gentlest movement counts, she says, and nothing needs to be earned by suffering.

Salma points out, to his great relief, that a sprained ankle is no reason to abandon the rest of the body, and she shows him how to train the parts that are not injured. Sitting upright in a sturdy chair, Omar lifts bags of rice above his head, pulls an elastic band towards his chest and works his stomach muscles, all without putting any weight on the bandaged foot. She adds that, with any injury, the advice of a doctor or physiotherapist should come first, and that Omar is fortunate to have one in the family.

After three weeks the swelling had gone, and Dr Rahman, having prodded the ankle with professional enthusiasm, told Omar that he could begin walking again as soon as it felt comfortable. He restarted with five minutes on flat ground, then ten, then fifteen, turning back the moment he felt a twinge, and resisting with great effort the old temptation to catch up on everything he had missed. Restarting gently, Salma had warned him, is the whole secret of recovering from a setback, and it is also the most boring part.

For his recovery, Dina and Lina gave Omar a simple step counter that clipped to his belt, wrapped in so much ribbon that it took him a full minute to find it. During the first week, with his short, careful walks and long hours at a desk, he averaged only about four thousand steps a day, which was far fewer than he had imagined. Numbers, Salma remarked, are very good at puncturing a comfortable story, and Omar resolved to take the deflation as a challenge rather than an insult.

In large studies, Salma says, the benefits of walking rise steadily with the number of steps taken each day, and then seem to level off at somewhere between seven and ten thousand, depending on the age of the people studied. The biggest gains come at the bottom, since going from two thousand steps to four thousand matters much more than going from ten to twelve. Omar, at four thousand, finds this both humbling and encouraging, which she says is the correct response.

The famous target of ten thousand steps, Salma tells him, is not a magic number at all. It is widely said to have begun as an advertising slogan for a Japanese step counter more than sixty years ago, long before researchers began to measure what daily walking actually does. The real message of the studies is gentler and more useful: more is better up to a point, and a little more than you do now is always a good place to start.

Omar discovers that extra steps are easy to find: he paces the room on the telephone, takes the stairs instead of the lift, and parks at the far end of the car park. Best of all is the walk he and Nadia take after dinner every evening, which begins as exercise and gradually turns into the best conversation of the day. By the end of August his average has risen to nearly seven thousand steps, and he has stopped thinking of it as a chore.

At the end of August, five weeks after the fall, Omar climbed the stone steps of Bell Hill again, placing each foot with the caution of a man crossing a frozen pond. He was slower than in June and stopped twice, and he was dismayed until Salma pointed out that fitness lost over a few weeks of rest usually returns much faster than it was first built. The summit, when they reached it, felt like a small victory, and the town below looked bright and forgiving.

At the September walk, with the first yellow leaves drifting across the steps, Salma reminded him that people spend about a third of their lives asleep. Most adults, she said, need somewhere between seven and nine hours a night, and Omar, who had been getting about six for as long as he could remember, suddenly became very attentive. He had always treated tiredness as a sign of seriousness, and he now suspected that it might simply be a sign of tiredness.

Poor sleep, Salma explains, is linked with heart disease, type 2 diabetes, low mood, accidents and problems with memory, and it makes the appetite harder to control. Many people who sleep too little insist that they feel perfectly fine, yet laboratory tests often show that their attention and judgement have slipped without their noticing. The tired brain, she says, is a poor judge of its own condition, which is rather like asking a broken thermometer to report its own temperature.

The first habit of good sleep, Salma says, is regularity: going to bed and getting up at roughly the same time every day, including weekends, so that the body's internal clock knows what to expect. Omar, who had always regarded Sunday morning as a sacred right to unlimited sleep, receives this news with a heavy sigh and the look of a man hearing about a tax. Within two weeks, however, he finds that waking at seven on Sundays gives him an extra hour of the best part of the day.

A bedroom that is dark, quiet and cool, Salma says, helps most people to fall asleep faster and to wake less often, because the body needs to drop its temperature a little in order to sleep. Omar hangs a pair of thick curtains, covers the small red light on the television with a piece of tape, and opens the window a few centimetres, much to the disgust of his wife, who likes her blankets warm. They settle on a compromise that involves a second blanket, a lower thermostat and a great deal of negotiation.

Daylight in the morning helps to set the body's clock, Salma explains, so Omar begins to drink his tea on the balcony each day and gives up his habit of reading the news in the dark. Caffeine drunk late in the afternoon, heavy meals close to bedtime and alcohol can all disturb sleep, and although a glass of wine may bring on drowsiness, it tends to make the second half of the night restless. He moves his last coffee to noon and is surprised how much he does not miss it.

Bright screens late at night, Salma continues, can make it harder to fall asleep, and the endless supply of news and messages on a phone is rarely calming. Omar agrees to charge his phone in the hallway, buys an alarm clock for almost nothing, and finds the first evening without a screen so peaceful that he reads an entire chapter of a novel. Nadia, who has been trying to achieve this for years, looks at him with deep respect.

On the way down the hill, Omar reluctantly passes on a confession from Nadia: that he snores like a lorry and sometimes seems to stop breathing for several seconds in the night. Salma explains that loud snoring with pauses in breathing, together with constant tiredness during the day, may be a sign of sleep apnoea, in which the airway repeatedly narrows during sleep. It can raise the risk of other health problems, she says, but it is treatable, and the person to ask is a doctor, never an internet quiz.

Omar mentioned the snoring to Dr Rahman, who arranged a simple test that he could carry out at home, with a small sensor clipped to his finger overnight. When the results came back they showed nothing worrying, and she told him, with some amusement, that his snoring was probably only snoring, which Nadia received with less relief than he did. For other people, she added, such a test can lead to effective treatment and a transformation in how they feel, which is exactly why it is worth asking.

Following Salma's suggestion, Omar keeps a sleep diary for a month, noting when he goes to bed, when he wakes and how he feels in the morning, and the pattern that emerges is more instructive than any lecture. On the days when he keeps to his routine and avoids late coffee, he falls asleep faster, wakes before the alarm and arrives at school in a better mood than the pupils deserve. By the end of September he is averaging nearly seven hours, and he has started to feel faintly smug.

On a Sunday afternoon Omar discovers the short nap, twenty minutes in the armchair with a blanket over his knees, and wakes feeling as though someone has refreshed his entire head. Salma warns him that a long nap late in the day can make night sleep harder, so the best nap is brief and early, and the best sleep is still the one at night. Sleep, she concludes, is not a reward for completing the plan but one of its main pillars, as important as any exercise.

On the October walk, Salma announces that she has no interest in strange diets, fashionable powders or any food that comes with a celebrity's face on the packet. Her advice is to eat mostly whole foods, such as vegetables, fruit, beans, fish, nuts and whole grains, and to eat less of the highly processed kind that has been so changed by factories that it hardly resembles its ingredients. Omar, who has just bought a family-sized bag of crisps at the foot of the hill, hides it behind his back.

Large studies have linked diets rich in highly processed food, such as sugary drinks, packaged snacks and ready meals, with a higher risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes and early death. It is difficult to prove that the food itself is to blame, since people who eat a lot of it may differ from others in many ways, but the pattern is consistent enough for Salma to give plain advice. She suggests that a person should look at the list of ingredients and be wary of anything that reads like a chemistry exam.

No single food is a miracle, Salma says, and no single treat is a disaster, because what counts is the pattern that a person keeps up for years. Eating in the Mediterranean style, with plenty of vegetables, beans, fruit, fish, nuts and olive oil and rather little red meat or sugar, has been linked in many studies with a lower risk of heart disease. It is not the only healthy pattern, she adds, but it has the advantage of being delicious, which makes it much easier to keep.

Omar and Nadia change the way they shop, wandering the supermarket on Saturday mornings with the fresh curiosity of tourists in a foreign city. They study labels, put beans, lentils, oats and frozen vegetables into the basket, and discover, to their astonishment, that eating well is often cheaper than eating badly. Nadia, who has always cooked beautifully, begins to experiment with a lentil soup that Lina describes as the best soup in the history of soup.

Muscle is built from protein, Salma says, and some experts suggest that older adults may need a little more of it than the young, because the ageing body becomes less efficient at turning food into muscle. Eggs, fish, beans, lentils, yoghurt and lean meat are all good sources, and spreading them across the day seems to work better than eating them all at dinner. People with kidney disease, however, are often given different advice, and they should talk to a doctor before changing anything.

Fibre, which comes from vegetables, fruit, beans and whole grains, feeds the helpful bacteria in the gut and is linked with a lower risk of heart disease and some cancers. Salma tells Omar that most people in wealthy countries eat much less of it than they should, and she suggests a rule too simple to forget: at least one vegetable on the plate at every meal. Omar adopts it at once, even at breakfast, where it produces a spectacular omelette.

Salma turns her attention to drinks, which she calls the most overlooked part of the modern diet, since one can of fizzy drink may hold most of the sugar a person should eat in a day. Water, plain tea and coffee without much sugar are all better choices, and in most studies moderate coffee drinking has not been found to be harmful for healthy adults. Omar, who has been buying a sweet drink from the school canteen every afternoon for twenty years, is silent for a moment, and then asks whether lemon counts.

Magazines and websites adore miracle diets, but Salma applies a simple test to any eating plan: could you follow it cheerfully for ten years, at birthdays and in bad weather? Patterns that involve fasting for part of the day or week suit some people and are being studied carefully, but so far the evidence that they do more for health than ordinary sensible eating is mixed. A plan that you abandon in March, she says, is worth much less than a modest one that you keep.

Fat that collects deep inside the belly is linked more strongly with heart disease and type 2 diabetes than fat stored elsewhere, so Salma takes a soft tape and measures Omar's waist at the middle. Many health bodies suggest that a waist measurement smaller than half a person's height is a useful rough guide, and she stresses that it is only one clue among many. Omar, who is slightly over the line, tries to take it as information and not as an insult.

Omar takes the result as information and not as an insult, which Salma says is the most mature response she has ever seen to a tape measure. Weight and waist are not the whole story, she adds, because muscle is heavy and useful, and a person can lose a little fat and gain a little muscle without the scales moving at all. He sets himself a gentle goal for the rest of the year: more movement, less sugar, one fewer biscuit with the afternoon tea, and no heroic promises.

On a cold, bright morning in November, with their breath hanging in the air like small clouds, Salma explained that some of the most dangerous conditions give no warning at all. A few simple measurements, taken by a doctor or a nurse, can reveal them years before any symptom appears, and the numbers are worth knowing in the same way that one knows the oil level of a car. Omar, who had never asked about a single number in his own body, felt a flicker of alarm and a flicker of interest.

The first number, Salma says, is blood sugar, because a level that stays too high for many years can quietly damage the eyes, the nerves, the kidneys and the heart without causing a single symptom. A simple blood test can show whether the level is normal, borderline or high, and a doctor can explain what the result means for a particular person and what, if anything, should be done. Catching a rise early, she adds, is the best way to turn type 2 diabetes from a likely future into an avoidable one for many people.

A few days later, Omar went to the clinic early in the morning without breakfast, rolled up his sleeve and watched the ceiling with great concentration while a nurse took several tubes of blood from his arm. She told him cheerfully that grown men were her most dependable fainters and that he had done better than most. The samples would be tested for blood sugar and for cholesterol, and Dr Rahman would explain the results at their next meeting.

The second number, Salma says, is blood pressure, which is the force with which the blood presses against the walls of the arteries as the heart pumps it round the body. When it stays too high, it usually produces no symptoms at all, yet over the years it raises the risk of heart attack, stroke and kidney disease, and that is why doctors call it the silent condition. The good news is that it is easy to measure, with a simple cuff around the arm, and in most cases it can be treated.

In her consulting room, Dr Rahman measured Omar's blood pressure twice, and both readings were a little higher than she would like to see in a man who was supposed to be getting fitter. She was not alarmed, since a visit to a clinic can itself raise the pressure, but she asked him to borrow a home monitor and to take a reading each morning for a week, sitting quietly. A pattern across several days, she said, tells a doctor far more than a single moment.

The third number, according to Salma, is cholesterol, a fatty substance carried in the blood, one kind of which, known as LDL, can build up in the walls of the arteries and slowly narrow them. She explains that, in general, the lower the LDL level, the lower the long-term risk, although the right target depends on a person's age, family history and other risks. A blood test shows the level, and only a doctor can say what it means for a particular patient.

The results came back mixed: Omar's blood sugar was normal, which pleased him, but his LDL cholesterol was a little higher than ideal, which did not. Dr Rahman explained that doctors judge the whole picture, including age, blood pressure and family history, and that for now she wanted him to continue his changes and to repeat the test in three months. If it stayed high, she added, they would discuss other options together, and the decision would be his.

For a week Omar measured his blood pressure every morning, sitting quietly with his back supported and his arm on the table, and wrote each result in a notebook. His readings at home turned out to be lower than the ones at the clinic, which Dr Rahman said was common, since some people become tense in a doctor's office, a phenomenon unkindly known as white-coat hypertension. She was pleased, although she asked him to have it checked again in the spring, because one good week is not a lifetime.

Salma, who has seen a great many anxious patients, warns Omar that more testing is not always better. Some expensive scans and blood panels, especially those sold directly to the public, find harmless oddities that are mistaken for diseases, and the result may be worry, further tests and even unnecessary treatment. A useful question for any test, she says, is what would be done differently depending on the result, and if the answer is nothing, it may be better left alone.

On the way down the hill, Omar copies his main numbers and the dates of each test onto a small card and slips it into his wallet, next to the card Dr Rahman had given him in June. Knowing a handful of numbers, Salma says, is a way of being in charge of your health rather than being at the mercy of it, and it is not at all the same as being afraid of them. Omar finds, rather to his surprise, that he feels calmer than he has for months.

Screening, Salma explains, means testing people who feel perfectly well in order to find certain diseases early, at a stage when they are often easier to treat. Many countries run national programmes that invite people for particular tests at particular ages, and she tells Omar that these invitations deserve to be taken seriously and not left on the kitchen table. Nadia, he realises, has a calendar full of such dates, all circled in blue, and he has never once asked what they were for.

Nadia, it turns out, has already been invited for breast screening, which is offered to women within a certain age range in many countries, and she takes Omar's sudden interest in good humour. The appointment itself lasts only a few minutes, she tells him afterwards, and it is slightly uncomfortable but entirely bearable. A week later a letter arrives with the result, which is clear, and the whole family feels a relief out of all proportion to the size of the envelope.

In some countries, people of Omar's age are invited to take a bowel screening test at home, and a small kit duly arrives in the post, accompanied by instructions that he reads three times with an expression of deep suspicion. He makes several jokes at his own expense, then does the test, seals it and sends it off, feeling that this is the most grown-up thing he has done all year. The result, when it comes, is normal, and although Salma reminds him that no test is a lifetime guarantee, he is glad he did it.

Other tests, Salma continues, include cervical screening for women, a check on any unusual moles, and in some countries scans for lung disease in long-term smokers. For certain cancers, such as prostate cancer, experts honestly disagree about whether routine testing of healthy men does more good than harm, because the tests can find slow-growing tumours that would never have caused trouble. The right answer, she says, is not to guess but to have an unhurried conversation with a doctor who knows your history.

Screening, Salma explains, has both benefits and costs, like almost everything in medicine, and an honest account of it has to include the costs. No test is perfect, false alarms happen, and some people are treated for conditions that would never have harmed them, yet for the main national programmes, experts have judged that the benefits to the population clearly outweigh the harms. The wise approach is to know what each test can and cannot do, and to make the decision with a doctor and not alone.

Mr Dalton, a teacher who smokes outside the school gate at break time, notices that Omar looks different and asks, with a mixture of envy and suspicion, what he has been doing. When Omar reports the conversation to Salma, she says that not smoking is among the best things that anyone can do for their health, and that quitting brings benefits at any age, even after decades of smoking. The risks begin to fall within months of stopping, she adds, and they keep falling for years.

Quitting is hard, Salma admits, because nicotine is powerfully addictive, but people who get support, such as a stop-smoking service, advice from a doctor or nicotine replacement, are much more likely to succeed than those who rely on willpower alone. Many people need several attempts before it lasts, and every attempt, she says, teaches them something about what triggers the craving. Mr Dalton takes the leaflet that Omar leaves on his desk, scowls at it, and puts it carefully in his pocket.

Salma is careful and calm on the subject of alcohol: health authorities agree that, as far as health goes, less is better than more, although their advice about specific limits varies from country to country. Heavy drinking raises the risk of liver disease, several cancers, high blood pressure and accidents, and even moderate drinking is not free of risk. Omar, who enjoys a glass of wine with dinner most evenings, decides to introduce several alcohol-free days each week and finds, to his mild surprise, that he does not miss it.

Not every risk to a long life comes from a slow disease, Salma points out, and some of the cheapest protections are also the most overlooked. Seat belts, cycle helmets, sunscreen and shade, and working smoke alarms all prevent harm for very little effort, and Omar, who has been riding his old bicycle without a helmet for decades, buys one on the way home. The best plans, she says, include the dull things that quietly stop bad things from happening.

Vaccines that health services recommend, such as those against influenza, pneumonia and shingles, prevent a great deal of serious illness in older adults, though each country has its own schedule and its own ages. Omar asks Dr Rahman which ones are meant for him, and she checks his record, answers patiently and books him an appointment for the following week. He leaves with a sore arm, a smile and the satisfaction of a man who has put another stone in the wall of his defences.

On the December walk, Omar admitted that what he feared most was not a heart attack but a slow loss of his own mind, and above all failing one day to recognise Lina. Salma listened without hurrying, and then told him that dementia, although it becomes more common with age, is not a normal part of growing older, and that many people live into their nineties with clear minds. The fear was reasonable, she said, but it did not need to run his life.

Everybody forgets where the keys are, or the name of the actor in the film, from time to time, Salma says, and that on its own is not dementia. The signs worth taking seriously are different: getting lost on a familiar street, repeating the same question within minutes, or struggling with tasks that were once easy, such as managing money or following a recipe. If such changes appear, or if the family becomes worried, it is sensible to see a doctor without delay, since some causes of memory trouble are treatable.

In 2024, Salma tells him, an international commission of experts reviewed the best available evidence and estimated that up to forty-five percent of dementia cases worldwide might be prevented or delayed by tackling fourteen risk factors. She writes the number on her notepad and draws a circle around it, because it is one of the few pieces of genuinely hopeful news in a gloomy subject. It is an estimate, she emphasises, and not a promise, and it describes populations and not individuals, but even as an estimate it deserves attention.

The first half of the list, Salma says, will sound familiar, because it names the usual enemies of the heart: high blood pressure, high LDL cholesterol, diabetes, smoking, alcohol, inactivity and excess weight. Hearing loss is also on the list, and it surprises Omar, who had always filed his ears under convenience and not under health. What is good for the heart, she observes, is very often good for the brain, which is convenient for anyone who wants to do both.

The rest of the list, she goes on, covers head injuries, depression, loneliness, air pollution, poor eyesight and having had little schooling early in life, which as a teacher Omar finds particularly interesting. Some of these, such as schooling or the air in a city, are beyond one person's control, but others are not, and he counts that he can work directly on most of the fourteen. It occurs to him that he has been using only a handful of the tools within his reach.

Salma is careful, as always, to be honest about the limits of what is known, because she has no wish to frighten him or to flatter him. The forty-five percent is an estimate, she says, and studies of this kind show links rather than proof, so nobody can promise that following the list will protect a particular person from dementia. Yet most of the steps are good for the heart, the bones, the mood and the sleep as well, which means that there is very little to lose and a great deal to gain.

Omar, who had been blaming his pupils for mumbling, books a hearing test at the local clinic and sits in a soundproof booth with headphones on, pressing a button whenever he hears a faint tone. The result shows a mild loss of the highest sounds, which is common at his age and explains why he has been struggling to follow conversations in the noisy school canteen. The audiologist tells him cheerfully that he is not as bad as he feared, and Nadia, quietly vindicated, says nothing at all.

Untreated hearing loss is linked with a higher risk of dementia, Salma explains, though nobody knows exactly why: perhaps because the strained brain has less energy left for memory, or perhaps because people who hear badly withdraw from company. Whether hearing aids can actually lower the risk is still being studied, and early results are promising without being conclusive. In the meantime they certainly help people to join in conversations, and a person who joins in is a person who is less alone.

Poor eyesight, Salma says, is linked with falls and with a higher risk of dementia, and many common eye problems, from cataracts to glaucoma, can be treated successfully if they are found early. Omar books an eye test, reads the letters on the chart with confidence until the bottom three lines, and is told by the optician that he needs glasses for reading. Lina, on seeing him in them, declares that he looks exactly like a professor, which he decides to take as a compliment.

At the top of the hill, as the winter sun slid behind the valley and turned the town to copper, Salma observed that the body and the brain are not two separate projects but one connected system. Whatever strengthens the heart, the lungs and the muscles usually protects the mind as well, she said, and the reverse is true: a mind that is lonely, sleepless or bored takes the body down with it. Before the next walk, she announced, he was to start learning something completely new, because the other half of brain health is using it.

Omar had dreamed of playing the guitar since he was nineteen, and the instrument had spent three decades leaning in a wardrobe, gathering dust and a faint sense of reproach. Inspired by Salma's challenge, he carried it to the Community Centre and signed up for lessons with a patient young man called Teo. The first thing Teo said, kindly, was that the guitar did not mind how late its owner had arrived.

The first lesson was humbling, because Omar's clumsy fingers refused to land on the right strings, and the chords he produced buzzed like an angry wasp trapped in a jar. His fingertips burned within ten minutes, and he began to suspect that he had made a ridiculous mistake. Teo, who had seen this look on many faces, only smiled and said that every guitarist alive had once sounded exactly like that.

On the January walk, with their breath hanging in white clouds above the steps, Omar described his sore fingers and his three wobbly chords. Salma was delighted, and explained that people who stay mentally active and keep learning demanding new things tend to have a lower risk of dementia in later life. She was careful to add that this is a link and not proof, since curious people may also differ from others in many other ways.

Omar confessed that he had also downloaded a brain-training app, which promised to sharpen his memory in only five minutes a day. Salma, who had read the studies, explained that such games reliably make people better at the games themselves, whereas the evidence that the gains spread to everyday memory and thinking is weak. Learning a real skill with real people, she said, is harder, slower and far more rewarding, which is exactly why it is likely to be better.

The best learning, according to Salma, has three ingredients, and she counted them off on her gloved fingers at the top of the steps. It should be new, difficult enough to make you stretch without making you quit, and practised in short, regular sessions, since ten minutes a day is worth more than an exhausting hour once a month. Anything that feels comfortable, she added with a grin, is probably something you have already learned.

At home, five-year-old Lina climbed onto her grandfather's lap, plucked the strings with the gravity of a concert pianist, and announced that she would like a song, please. Nothing in Omar's life had ever motivated him so quickly, and for a week he practised a simple tune after dinner until the chords stopped buzzing. When he finally played it all the way through, Lina clapped, frowned, and asked whether he could do a faster one.

Halfway up the hill that month, Omar and Salma overtook a small woman in a green coat, who was climbing steadily with a wooden stick and refused to be hurried. She introduced herself as Mrs Hale, aged eighty-three, and announced with some pride that she made the climb two mornings a week, stopping on every tenth step to admire the view. Omar, who had stopped four times on his first attempt, felt his respect for her swell with every step.

At the bottom of the hill, Mrs Hale led them to a ragged strip of soil beside the pavement, which she had turned into a street garden full of herbs, beans and winter cabbages. She had only begun growing vegetables at the age of seventy-five, she told them, after her husband died, and her one regret was that she had not started fifty years earlier. Her neighbours now left her seed packets on the gate, and she repaid them with parsley.

Omar, never one to refuse a spade, volunteered to dig a new bed, and within ten minutes he was warm, muddy and rather pleased with himself. Salma observed that gardening combines gentle movement, fresh air and daylight with a reason to come back tomorrow, and that heavy tasks such as digging can count as strength work. She added that the back must stay straight and the knees must do their share, while Mrs Hale, supervising from a folding chair, corrected his technique twice.

At the top, Omar unzipped his guitar case, balanced the instrument on his knee and played his simple tune for Salma and Mrs Hale, with only two audible mistakes and one long, brave pause. Salma clapped louder than the performance deserved, and said that it was the doing, rather than the cleverness, that mattered, and that he should never stop being a beginner at something. A passing walker dropped a coin into the open case, which Omar decided to count as his first professional fee.

On the bench near the top, Salma watched the other walkers pass in pairs and trios, and then said, in her most careful voice, that long-lasting loneliness is linked with a higher risk of early death, heart disease and dementia. The size of the risk in some large reviews is comparable to that of well-known habits such as heavy smoking, though the studies are hard to compare and nobody can be sure how much of it is cause. What is certain, she said, is that nobody ever lay awake wishing they had seen fewer friends.

Omar went to see Hamid, who was now walking every morning and looked ten years younger than he had in hospital. Over tea, Hamid confessed that the best part of his rehabilitation programme had not been the exercise machines but the other patients, who understood without being told exactly how frightened he had been. Samira, pouring a second cup, added that her husband had talked more in those six weeks than in the previous six years.

That evening, scrolling idly through his phone, Omar came upon the name of Yusuf, with whom he had shared a flat at university and a great many late-night arguments about football. They had not spoken for two years, not because of any quarrel, but because both of them had been busy, and busyness has a way of turning into distance without anyone deciding it should. Omar stared at the name for a long minute, then pressed the green button before he could change his mind.

The first minute of the call was stiff and apologetic, with both men insisting that it was entirely their own fault. Then Yusuf mentioned an old professor's terrible moustache, Omar snorted with laughter, and the two years seemed to fold up and disappear. By the end of the call they had promised to climb Bell Hill together on Saturday, and Nadia, hearing her husband laugh like a student, smiled quietly in the doorway.

Strong, warm relationships, Salma told them as they climbed, are linked with better health and a longer life in many large studies. Part of the reason may be simple, because friends encourage each other to get outside, notice when something is wrong and make the bad days easier to bear. Another part may run the other way, she cautioned, since people who feel well find it easier to keep their friendships going.

At the foot of the hill one Tuesday evening, Omar was introduced to Mr Okafor, a tall man of seventy-one with a booming laugh and a fluorescent yellow jacket. He led a group called the Tuesday Walkers, a cheerful band of about a dozen people who climbed Bell Hill every week, whatever the weather. Anyone could join, Mr Okafor boomed, provided they were willing to be teased about their pace.

To his surprise, Omar discovered that he walked faster in company than he ever did alone, because the conversation took his mind off his calves and the group's rhythm pulled him along. He passed the talk test comfortably, since he could chat throughout but would not have managed a song. Studies suggest that people stick with exercise for longer when they do it with others, and the Tuesday Walkers, who had not missed a week in six years, were the living proof.

After each climb, the Tuesday Walkers crowded into Rosa's Cafe at the foot of the hill, where Rosa herself served tea, toast and a running commentary on everyone's love life. A quiet widower named Gil told Omar, over his second cup, that the group was the main reason he left the house in winter, and that his doctor had noticed the change before he did. Omar looked around the steamy room and understood that the tea was only half of what was being served.

At Rosa's, Salma wrote a short list on a paper napkin and slid it across the table, saying that the quality of friendships matters far more than their number. A few close people are enough, she said, and the upkeep is cheaper than anyone expects: a call, a message, a walk or a shared meal will keep most friendships alive. Omar folded the napkin carefully, as if it were a prescription, and put it in his wallet beside his cards.

On Saturday evening, Omar's modest flat held the loudest and happiest dinner it had seen in years, because Nadia, who adored cooking for a crowd, had produced a feast of rice, roasted vegetables and lentil stew. Hamid, Samira, Yusuf, Mr Okafor and Salma squeezed around the table, passing dishes and interrupting one another, while Lina sat under it with a biscuit. Salma, raising a glass of water, said that this, and not any exercise machine, was one of the finest parts of the whole plan.

That winter Hill Road School was bracing itself for an inspection, and Omar, who was in charge of the older pupils' reports, was working late and sleeping badly. When he complained to Salma on the phone, she told him that stress is a normal and even useful response, because a short burst of it sharpens attention and helps us to meet a deadline. The trouble begins, she said, only when the alarm never switches off and the body is never allowed to rest.

Stress that lasts for weeks and months, Salma explained, is linked with poor sleep, low mood and higher blood pressure, partly through the body's alarm chemicals and partly through the habits that stress tends to bring with it. Tired and worried people reach for sugary snacks and extra coffee, skip their walks and stay up too late, which makes the next day harder still. Omar recognised every item on the list with a sinking heart, and especially the biscuit that he happened to be holding.

Nobody can remove all stress from a life, Salma said, and anyone who promises to is selling something. A better goal is recovery, meaning the habits that let the body come back down to calm after a hard day, and the evidence is good that exercise, time outdoors, close friends and enough sleep all help. She pointed out, with a small smile, that these happened to be items already on the plan.

She also taught him a simple trick, which was to breathe in gently through the nose for about four seconds and out through the mouth for about six, and to repeat the cycle for a few minutes. Some studies suggest that slow breathing of this kind helps people to feel calmer, although the evidence is modest and nobody should expect a miracle. Omar tried it in the staff room before a difficult meeting, and found that, at the very least, it gave him something to do other than panic.

On his lunch break, instead of eating a sandwich at his desk, Omar walked twice around the park beside the school, noticing the bare branches, a pair of magpies and the particular green of the moss on the bench. Studies link time in green places with a better mood and lower stress, though it is hard to say how much of the effect comes from the greenery and how much from simply leaving the desk. Whatever the reason, Omar's shoulders came down from around his ears for the first time that week.

A few days later, Samira phoned Omar to say, in a voice kept low so that her husband would not hear, that Hamid had been flat and silent for weeks despite his good progress. Omar passed the news to Salma, who said gently that low mood is common after a heart attack and is a real health matter and not a weakness of character. The best step, she said, was for Hamid to mention it to his doctor or rehabilitation nurse, because help exists and works.

Omar sat beside his friend on the garden bench and, for once, resisted the teacher's urge to fix, advise or cheer him up. He simply listened while Hamid spoke slowly about his fear of another attack, and afterwards the two men walked to the corner of the street and back at the pace of an old dog. Hamid said that it was the best conversation he had had in weeks, though Omar privately thought that he had said almost nothing.

Salma had told Omar that low mood which lasts most of the day for two weeks or more is a good reason to speak to a doctor, and that nobody should wait until it feels unbearable. Hamid, nudged by Samira and by Omar's quiet example, finally made the appointment and described how he had been feeling. His doctor arranged support and regular check-ins, and Hamid reported afterwards that talking about it had been less frightening than keeping it inside.

A sense of purpose, said Salma, as they watched Mrs Hale watering her cabbages with great dignity, is linked in several studies with a longer and healthier life. The link probably runs both ways, since people who feel well find it easier to pursue their goals, and people with goals have more reason to look after themselves. Purpose, she added, does not need to be grand, because a garden, a grandchild or a Tuesday walking group will do very nicely.

Omar asked himself, with some embarrassment, what exactly his own purpose might be, and was surprised by how quickly the answer arrived: his pupils, his family and the friends he was learning to keep. Combining the first of these with his new habits, he chalked a notice on the school board announcing the Hill Road Walkers, a Thursday club for pupils and teachers. Eleven children and three nervous colleagues turned up, and Mr Dalton, who smoked, watched from the doorway with his arms folded.

On the February walk, the steps were slick with frost, and Omar, gripping the rail, admitted that he felt overwhelmed. Walking, lifting, sleeping, eating, friends, check-ups, learning and calm had each seemed sensible when explained, but together they made a list so long that he could not imagine keeping it up on a rainy Wednesday. Salma, who had been expecting this complaint for weeks, nodded as though he had passed a test.

Nobody overhauls an entire life in a week, Salma said, and those who attempt it usually founder by the third Friday and abandon the project in disgust. A far wiser strategy is to alter one or two things at a time, let them settle until they feel like an ordinary part of the day, and only then introduce something new. Omar, who had been performing roughly eleven resolutions badly, felt a great weight lift from his shoulders.

Salma proposed the humblest instrument imaginable, which was a small notebook with a single line allotted to each day. Every evening Omar was to record whether he had walked briskly, whether he had lifted or squatted, and how well he had slept, with no further elaboration or ambition. A pencil, she observed, costs less than any gadget, requires no software updates and has never once run out of battery.

A notebook works, Salma explained, because it turns vague impressions into evidence: after a few weeks Omar would be able to see for himself whether his walking, his lifting and his sleep were improving. She added a warning, however, that numbers are guides and not judges, since a bad night or a missed day says very little about a whole year. A person who obsesses over every figure has simply found a new way to feel anxious.

The most reliable trick of all, said Salma, is to fasten a new habit to an old one that happens without thinking, so that the old one acts as a reminder. Omar made a tea at least five times a day, and he decided that every time the kettle was boiling he would stand on one leg, holding the counter if he had to. By the end of the first week he did it without remembering to remember, which was exactly the point.

Make it small and make it easy, Salma urged, because the hardest part of any habit is the first two minutes. Omar placed his trainers beside the front door, hung a rucksack of books on the same hook as his coat, and promised himself that on bad days he would do only two minutes and then permit himself to stop. Most days, to his quiet amusement, the two minutes stretched into twenty, and the trainers were on his feet before he had decided anything.

Nadia, who had borrowed three books on habits from the library, reported that a new routine takes time to feel automatic, and that the popular claim of twenty-one days has little behind it. One well-known study found that it took about two months on average, although individuals ranged from a few weeks to many months, so Omar should be patient with himself. The lesson, she concluded, with a librarian's satisfaction, was that nobody should be surprised when a habit does not stick in a fortnight.

One rainy evening Omar was simply too tired, and he stared at the empty line in his notebook as though it were a crime scene. Salma, when he confessed, laughed and said that a single missed day does no harm to anyone, and that the real danger is only the second miss, which has a habit of becoming a third. A sensible rule of thumb, she said, is to never miss twice, although nobody has proved it.

Soon the whole family had joined in, in the way that families do, without announcement and with a certain amount of competition. Nadia began her own notebook and Dina sent photographs of her evening walks, while Lina appointed herself inspector of the fridge calendar. She awarded a gold star for every day he moved and a stern frown for every day he did not, and the stars were slowly beginning to outnumber the frowns.

At the end of the month Omar repeated his two simple tests, the chair stands and the one-legged balance, and compared the results with the figures from the summer. He rose from the chair five times noticeably faster than before, and balanced on one leg for about twenty seconds, against the wobbling five that had once embarrassed him at the kitchen counter. Nadia, passing with a tray of cups, laughed out loud at the sight of her husband standing like a heron beside the whistling kettle.

In the staff room, a colleague pushed his phone across the table to show Omar a glossy advertisement for an anti-ageing pill, which promised to turn back the clock and cost about as much as a month's rent. Omar, who had spent eleven months learning to be sceptical, photographed the screen and sent it to Salma with a single question mark. Her reply arrived within the minute and consisted of a laughing face and the words, call me tonight.

That evening Salma told him, with her usual calm, that no supplement or medicine has so far been proved to slow ageing in people. Many claims rest on experiments with cells in dishes or animals in cages, which are a long way from a middle-aged teacher, and others on a single trial that nobody has repeated. The most reliable anti-ageing product, she said, is still the dull one on the plan.

Salma was careful not to condemn all supplements, because a few are genuinely useful for particular people and particular problems. When a blood test shows a real lack, for example of vitamin D or vitamin B12, a doctor may recommend a supplement, and some other groups, such as pregnant women, are advised to take specific ones. Anyone on regular medicine should check with a doctor or pharmacist first, she warned, because even natural products can interfere with prescribed ones.

Salma, who described herself as a connoisseur of nonsense, taught Omar to read the warning signs of hype. Words such as miracle, secret and breakthrough are suspicious, as are glowing personal stories offered in place of proper studies, a single expensive product that claims to fix everything, and any promise of quick results. When a claim sounds too good to be true, she said, there is usually a price tag standing very close behind it.

That is not to say that the science of ageing is a fraud, Salma continued, because serious researchers around the world are studying why bodies wear out. They work with worms, flies and mice, which live only weeks or years and can be watched from birth to death, while a few medicines used for other conditions are being tested in people. The work is fascinating, she said, but it is early, and early results have a way of shrinking.

Many findings in animals, Salma explained, fail to carry over to people, for reasons that are not hard to guess. A mouse lives for about two years and a person for many decades, laboratory mice eat measured food in controlled rooms, and a medicine that helps a mouse may do nothing for a human. Excitement about a single early study, she said, is the surest sign that someone is about to be disappointed.

Back at home, Omar did something that appealed to the schoolteacher in him and added up the cost of his entire plan on a sheet of squared paper. Walking shoes, a rucksack of old books, a bag of lentils, a packet of oats and a month's supply of sleep came to scarcely more than the price of one bottle of the miracle pills. The plan that Salma had been describing all year, he realised with some surprise, was one of the cheapest in the world.

One chilly morning Mr Dalton, the colleague who had smoked outside the school gate for twenty years, took Omar aside and announced that he had joined a free stop-smoking service and had not touched a cigarette in three weeks. With the help of a counsellor and some nicotine patches, he said, it was the first attempt that had ever felt possible, and he had already saved enough money to buy a new pair of shoes. His morning cough, he added proudly, had nearly gone, and he could now climb the stairs at school without wheezing like a kettle.

Money is not the enemy, Salma conceded over sandwiches and a flask of tea. It can pay for glasses, hearing aids or a blood pressure monitor, all of which genuinely help, but it cannot buy fitness, which must be earned slowly, one ordinary day after another. Nobody, she said, has ever been able to pay somebody else to climb the steps for them.

On the cover of his notebook, in the careful capitals of a man who has taught handwriting for thirty years, Omar wrote that health is earned and not bought. The best investment in the whole plan, he reflected, was not money but ordinary time, spent a little at a time on walking, lifting, sleeping and sitting with people he loved. It was a quieter kind of wealth than the advertisements promised, and, he suspected, a good deal more reliable.

In the last grey weeks of winter, when the mornings were black and the rain seemed to have no intention of stopping, Omar caught a heavy cold that swiftly deepened into flu. He spent five days in bed under three blankets, missing school, the Tuesday Walkers and his guitar lesson, and listening to the water running down the window. Nadia brought him soup and, with great restraint, did not mention the word plan.

Even after the fever had gone, Omar found that he lacked the energy, and also the will, to start again, and ten days passed with scarcely a step or a squat. The notebook lay untouched on the kitchen table, the trainers gathered dust beside the door, and a heavy mood of guilt settled over him that was somehow worse than the flu itself. It seemed impossible to him now that he had ever climbed Bell Hill without stopping, or that he would ever do so again.

Salma arrived with a bag of oranges and, to Omar's surprise, delivered no lecture whatsoever. Setbacks, she said, are not a failure of the plan but a part of it, because illness, injury, work and weather interrupt everyone sooner or later, and a good plan includes the way back. What matters is not whether you fall off the horse, she said, but how kindly and how quickly you climb on again.

Returning to exercise after an illness, Salma explained, can be guided by a common rule of thumb about where the symptoms sit. If they are mild and above the neck, such as a runny nose or a sore throat, gentle activity is usually acceptable, but a fever, a chesty cough or aching all over means rest. It was a guide and not a guarantee, she added, and anyone who felt unsure, or whose symptoms lingered, should ask a doctor.

Following Salma's advice, Omar resumed at about half his old level, with ten minutes of easy walking on the flat and not a single hill in sight. He was astonished to find himself puffing after the second street, as if the fitness he had spent months building had evaporated in a week. Salma had warned him that this was normal, and that, once started, fitness often returns faster than it was first built.

Within a fortnight Omar was almost back at his old level, walking briskly again to school and climbing the stairs without stopping. Salma, who loved a pattern, said that fitness lost during a short break often returns more quickly than it was first built, though a longer layoff takes correspondingly longer to recover. Omar wrote this sentence in capital letters in the notebook, underlined it twice and gave it the title, the good news.

At the Community Centre, in a quiet corner of the gym, Omar met Iris, who used a wheelchair and lifted weights three times a week with the concentration of an Olympic athlete. She told him cheerfully that she had been inactive for years after an accident, and that the right equipment and a patient trainer had changed her life. Studies have shown that even people in their eighties and nineties can gain real strength from training, Salma said afterwards, so almost everyone can find some movement that suits them, if they start gently and take professional advice.

On a notepad, Salma drew a staircase and labelled each step with a stage of life and its chief priority. In the thirties and forties, she said, build lasting habits, in the fifties and sixties protect muscle and bone, and in the seventies and beyond preserve balance, strength and independence. The details differ with the person, she added, but the direction of travel is the same for everyone, and it is always upward.

Slowly, the dark weeks passed, and the mornings crept earlier and paler, until one day Omar woke to find a stripe of sunlight across the bedroom floor. Walking in the morning light, which also helps to set the body's clock, lifted his mood almost as reliably as the exercise did, and Nadia noticed that he had begun to hum in the kitchen again. Salma had said that if the low feeling lasted, he should talk to a doctor, and he was glad that it had not come to that.

In Mrs Hale's street garden the first white snowdrops had pushed through the cold soil, and Mrs Hale, bent over them with her stick, looked as pleased as if she had invented them. Omar stood beside her for a long moment, feeling the particular gladness of a person who has had a bad month and come out of it, and then took out his phone to send Salma a message. The year was nearly complete, and he wanted the final climb on his calendar.

A year had passed since the bargain, and it was March again, with a mild breeze and the first green haze on the trees. Two weeks after his fifty-third birthday, Omar stood with Salma at the foot of Bell Hill and looked up at the same one hundred and sixty stone steps that had once made him gulp. He did not feel confident, exactly, but he felt something quieter and more useful, which was familiarity.

Omar set off at a steady, comfortable pace, counting each step silently as he went, and Salma, who normally had something to say about everything, followed a few paces behind and kept her remarks to herself. By the fortieth step he was breathing deeply but evenly, and by the eightieth he realised that his legs had not yet complained. The hill, which a year earlier had felt like an enemy, now felt rather like an old acquaintance.

Halfway up stood the little bench where, a year earlier, Omar had slumped and gasped with his hand pressed to his ribs. This time he glanced at it, smiled at it, and walked straight past without altering his pace, and Salma, watching his broad back go ahead, permitted herself a small private smile. There are moments, she thought, when a person's whole year is contained in a single bench.

At the top, Omar arrived without having stopped a single time, a fact that he announced to the sky in a voice somewhat higher than normal. He was breathing hard, certainly, but he could still speak in complete sentences, which meant, as Salma pointed out, that he had passed the talk test with a respectable mark. They sat on the wall and drank tea from the flask while the town spread out below them like a map.

Salma, who had not forgotten the floor test in the living room a year earlier, asked him to sit cross-legged on the grass and then rise without the help of his hands. Omar crossed his shins, drew a breath, rocked forward and stood up in one wobbling movement, and then laughed aloud like a boy. It was, he thought, the smallest victory of his life and quite possibly the most satisfying.

Omar, flushed with success, asked the question that had been following him all year: how many extra years had he gained? Salma answered honestly that nobody could tell him, because nobody can measure the heart attack that did not happen. No plan on earth can promise a long life, since genes and luck take a hand, she added, but a good plan improves the odds and, even more important, the quality of the years.

Omar counted what he had gained on his fingers and soon ran out of them. There were stairs without stopping, the floor without his hands, sounder sleep, new friends, an old friend won back and a guitar tune that Lina could actually recognise. The list was longer than he had expected, and none of it had required a miracle, an expensive machine or a heroic act of will, only, he realised, a great many ordinary Tuesdays.

Salma took out her pen and, on the back of an old appointment card, wrote the whole plan as six short lines. Move often, lift something heavy twice a week, sleep well, eat mostly real food, keep your friends close, and have your regular check-ups, and ask a doctor when you are unsure. That was the entire secret, she said, and the only difficult part about it was that it could not be bought, only done.

Voices drifted up the steps, and the whole crowd came into view: Nadia with the picnic basket, Dina with his guitar case, and Mrs Hale, bringing up the rear with her stick. Hamid, who had climbed every step on his own two feet, shook Omar's hand, while Samira and Mr Okafor cheered and Lina ran ahead of them all. Omar played his tune for them, and when Lina asked whether he would still carry her at ten, he said that she should ask again in five years and that he would be ready.

Omar's one-page plan went onto the fridge, beside Lina's gold stars, and there it stayed. It is a modest piece of paper, and it promises nothing, which is exactly why Salma trusted it. Like everything in this book, it is general information and is not medical advice, so anyone with a health condition, an injury or regular medicine should talk to a doctor first.
